questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The gold ground of the San Vitale apse, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: explain why a gold mosaic ground refuses recession and what that does to the figures on it
questions.stem: In the apse mosaic of San Vitale at Ravenna, made about 547, the emperor Justinian stands frontally at the head of a procession of clergy and soldiers. Behind and beneath the figures the ground is gold glass tesserae set in even courses, no cast shadow appears anywhere, and no architecture is drawn behind them. What does that gold ground do to the space the procession occupies?

options.text: It locates the procession inside a real building, since gold glass in mosaic was only ever used to record a sunlit interior
options.misconception: treats gold as a way of rendering a lit room rather than a way of suspending place

options.text: It creates a deep illusionistic space, since the even courses of tesserae make the gold behave like a receding floor and wall
options.misconception: believes a regular gold mosaic ground produces illusionistic recession, when gold is exactly what denies it

options.text: It holds the figures in a shallow, non-receding field, so the scene reads as a presentation rather than a place with depth
It cancels the modelling of the figures, since a featureless ground removes the light and shade the faces depend upon
options.misconception: supposes a plain ground destroys modelling, when the modelling is carried by the tesserae of the bodies themselves

questions.explanation: A gold ground is not a description of any lit surface; it is a decision about what kind of space the image inhabits. Because the field is even in value, carries no cast shadow, and is interrupted by no drawn architecture, it supplies no cue for distance, and the figures therefore have nothing to recede from. They stand forward on a surface that reads as the limit of the image rather than as the floor of a room. The effect on the subject is direct. Justinian is not shown standing in a church; he is shown holding a bowl of bread, and the gold takes that offering out of any particular hour and place and gives it the character of a presentation, a thing offered to be looked at and not merely recorded. Note the negative half of the reasoning too. The modelling of the faces and drapery is not weak but very strong, worked in graded rows of tesserae that shift in value, so a plain ground does not flatten a mosaic; it isolates the bodies that stand on it. And because the field denies depth, it also denies architecture, which is why the setting of this apse is supplied by the actual curve of the half-dome and by the light entering its clerestory windows rather than by anything painted.
questions.hint: Ask what a surface with no shadow and no drawn architecture can tell you about how far back a figure stands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The hem of the Theodora panel at San Vitale
questions.learningObjective: describe how the lower edge of a Byzantine mosaic carries a second subject
questions.stem: The facing panel of the San Vitale apse mosaic, Ravenna, about 547, shows the empress Theodora with her attendants. Along the bottom edge of her purple robe runs a band of small white shapes, and at the hem itself three tiny figures in coloured cloaks appear to walk in procession. What is that band doing at the foot of the robe?

options.text: Recording the cost of the robe, since a list of small devices would show the value of the material and its embroidery
options.misconception: reads a figural border as an inventory of value, as though it itemised price rather than told a story

options.text: Signing the work, since a craftsman places a miniature self-portrait in the border of a commission he finished
options.misconception: treats a border figure as a maker's signature, a convention the mosaic does not use

options.text: Fixing the scale of the empress, since tiny figures at the hem give a standard for measuring how large she is
options.misconception: assumes the small figures are a scale bar for the main figure, which no mosaic uses that way

options.text: Carrying a second subject, since the three figures at the hem read as a procession that extends the imagery down into the border

questions.explanation: The hem of Theodora's robe is a second picture, and it is the clearest case in early Byzantine mosaic of a field that is a boundary also being used as a place. A pattern of white gem shapes alone would be ornament, and ornament at an edge has the job of stopping the eye from sliding out of the composition. But three of those shapes resolve into coloured cloaks and feet, and they read as a procession moving along the lower edge. Once that happens the border becomes a place with its own subject, and the image gains a second register without a second frame. The device does several things at once. It turns the hem of a garment into a landscape, so the empress's robe becomes the ground on which something happens, and the second subject is drawn at the scale appropriate to its position, small because it is far away and low, not small because it is unimportant. It also connects the two facing panels: the Justinian panel opposite has soldiers and a very thin, dark architectural strip at its base, so the lower zone of the whole apse carries architecture on one side and a figural procession on the other. And it refuses the idea that a border is inert ground. The two are the same thing here, and the eye is given a second thing to read precisely where a tapestry or a painted panel would have given it a stop.
questions.hint: Ask whether the small shapes at the hem are a repeating ornament or can be resolved into figures with clothes and feet.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: explain why the Good Shepherd in a fifth-century mosaic is beardless and monumental
questions.stem: The mosaic decoration of the Galla Placidia mausoleum at Ravenna, made about 425, shows a Good Shepherd standing frontally in a short tunic, holding a staff, with a sheep at his feet and four rivers of Paradise flowing below him from a rock. The shepherd is beardless, dressed in imperial gold, and about as large as the other figures in the ceiling. What does that scale and dress do to what the image is about?

options.text: It presents the shepherd as a ruler rather than a herdsman, so the image claims that power and salvation are shown in the same figure
It argues for a classical subject, since a beardless shepherd is the Greek type and the gold is the Roman type
options.misconception: treats beard and gold as proof of two sources rather than as one deliberate blend

options.text: It identifies the patron, since a beardless young ruler in gold must be the dead princess shown as a shepherd
options.misconception: reads a conventional divine type as a specific portrait of the patron

options.text: It shows that the mosaic was copied from a Roman sarcophagus, since imperial dress and frontal pose are what Roman reliefs do
options.misconception: jumps from a shared convention to a copied source, where a convention needs no borrowing

questions.explanation: The gold tunic and the frontality are doing the work, and the missing beard is part of the same decision. In a fifth-century mosaic a shepherd rendered as a beardless youth in gold is not a farmer; it is a statement about authority, and the size of the figure in a field of other figures sets that authority at the same level as everything else on the ceiling rather than above it. The four rivers below complete the argument without any further explanation, because in this imagery flowing water is the sign of the paradise the shepherd rules, and the rock from which they issue is the same rock that stands for the whole commanded place. Three things this image is not doing are worth separating out. It is not a portrait of the princess whose name the mausoleum takes, because a divine type is being shown rather than a person, and the details of the type are conventional. It is not evidence that a Roman sarcophagus was copied, because imperial dress and frontality were current Byzantine practice and a convention travels without a source. And it is not a lesson on two subjects, Greek and Roman, in one figure, because the youth and the gold are read together as a single statement. The test to apply is simple: if a viewer could not name the patron from this figure, but every viewer would read authority from it, the figure is a type and its scale is part of its meaning.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure reads as someone tending sheep or as someone who rules, and what the missing beard contributes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Encaustic handling in the Sinai icon of the Virgin and Child
questions.learningObjective: distinguish encaustic panel painting from the gold-ground convention
questions.stem: An icon in the monastery of St Catherine on Mount Sinai shows the enthroned Virgin and Child flanked by the soldier saints Theodore and George. The surface has no gold ground: the background is a plain warm brown, and the flesh is built from soft strokes that are worked, blended and picked out in opaque white, so that the faces look modelled rather than described. The panel is dated to the sixth or seventh century. What does the absence of a gold ground and the softness of the flesh tell you?

options.text: That the icon was made for private devotion rather than for a church, since a plain ground removes the altar function
options.misconception: supposes function follows from the ground colour, when a work can be made for a church in any convention

options.text: That the painter worked in wax on wood with a brush, and that the modelled flesh records a painter trained where modelled portraiture was practised
That the icon is unfinished, since a background of plain brown is what remains when a gold layer has been lost
options.misconception: reads a deliberate plain ground as lost gilding rather than as a choice

options.text: That the icon is a copy, since original panel icons of that century are always painted on a gold ground
options.misconception: treats a single convention as a test of originality rather than one option among several

questions.explanation: Two things are being read at once, and they are different kinds of evidence. The first is medium and technique. Encaustic is pigment bound in hot wax and applied with a brush, and the marks it leaves can be modelled: laid in, blended while warm, and then picked out in opaque light. That is what the description reports in the cheeks, the brows and the chain of highlights down the nose. A gold ground, by contrast, is a different kind of decision about surface, and its absence here is not a loss. A background of plain warm brown pushes the figures forward and lets the modelling do the work, so the two are alternatives rather than stages of one method. The second thing is training. Faces modelled with light and shade, and faces with the fronts lit from one side and shadows in the other, belong to a pictorial world in which such modelling was practised; the saints here wear late antique dress, and the Virgin is enthroned frontally with the Child at her breast, which is a subject not derived from the same tradition as the shading. The church the icon came from is Byzantine and gold-grounded in its other panels, which is exactly why the difference is informative. An image that models flesh against plain ground in a gold-grounded church is making a deliberate choice about how the person is to be seen, not recording a local shortage.
questions.hint: Ask what wax bound paint can do that a gilded ground cannot, and what a plain background is doing to the space.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Continuous narrative in the Vienna Genesis
questions.learningObjective: explain how a continuous narrative scroll handles several moments in one field
questions.stem: The Vienna Genesis, an illuminated manuscript of about the early sixth century on purple-dyed vellum, carries a Genesis cycle in which the same figures appear more than once inside a single painted zone: a man leading a woman appears again further along, and the pair recur a third time. Separating the scenes is thin framing, the repetition of a wall or a piece of ground, and the same costumes recur. What is being asked of the viewer?

options.text: To infer that the manuscript is unfinished, since a painted zone should never contain a figure more than once
options.misconception: treats a compositional rule of some books as a test of completion everywhere

options.text: To identify a single moment precisely, since the painter worked to make each episode self-contained for a reader in a hurry
options.misconception: supposes repetition serves isolation, when it is what makes a sequence legible

options.text: To read a sequence left to right, since the repetition of figures separates a set of episodes that share one continuous landscape
To compare two different artists, since a change of costume and of handling between episodes marks a change of hand
options.misconception: reads variation inside one zone as evidence of several hands without any comparison

questions.explanation: The device is called continuous narrative, and its logic is that a single continuous zone of landscape or architecture holds several moments at once. Because the same personage recurs, the eye has to be taught how to separate them, and it is taught by the things that do not recur: a wall, a door, a strip of ground, a shift in the pattern of a garment. A reader trained on this book learns to scan a band of landscape and to register each appearance of a figure as a new moment, so the order is given by the layout rather than by separate frames. Two consequences follow, and they are the reason the device matters. First, the book becomes a sequence in a very literal sense, so the reader experiences a story unfolding across a surface rather than turning from compartment to compartment, and the physical experience of a codex page is a landscape read sideways. Second, repetition is not a failure of economy but the mechanism, which is why the criterion for a competent rendering in this technique is not individual figure quality but whether each episode is separable. The purple ground is a separate matter and should not be confused with any of this. It is the costliest support available, dyed before the vellum was written on, and it is a statement about the value of the book and the rank of its patron rather than about how the episodes are laid out. Nor does a figure appearing twice in a zone tell you a hand changed, because a change of hand is argued by comparison with other pages, not by a costume that is deliberately the same.
questions.hint: Ask why the painter repeats a figure instead of drawing two separate frames, and what the repeated figure is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Silver ink and decorative initials in the Rossano Gospels
questions.learningObjective: explain why a manuscript's ornament can carry as much weight as its pictures
questions.stem: The Rossano Gospels, a Greek manuscript of the sixth century, is written in uncial script with silver ink and has no evangelist portraits and no narrative pictures. Its ornament is in the initials, which are built from small animal and plant forms locked into a lattice of squares, filled with bands of colour, and separated from one another by broad bars of purple and gold. What does the decoration of this book declare about it?

options.text: That the book is unfinished, since a Gospel book of that century ought to have carried evangelist portraits and does not
options.misconception: reads one book's omissions as damage, when several books of the period have no portraits

options.text: That the animal forms are symbolic of the evangelists, since a man and a lion always denote Matthew and Mark
options.misconception: applies an evangelist-symbol code to decorative initials that are not portraits of anything

options.text: That the text is unimportant, since a book that spends its effort on decoration must be valued for its ornament alone
options.misconception: assumes lavish ornament means the text was not valued, when the two are the same claim

options.text: That writing itself is the image, so effort has been spent on the letterforms and their frames rather than on figures beside the text

questions.explanation: This book is a useful corrective to the habit of expecting pictures. Some of the earliest Gospel manuscripts are essentially illuminations of the script itself: the text is carried by letters of a monumental size, and the ornamental energy goes into the opening letters, which are laid out as tiled fields of interlaced animals, birds, vine scrolls and small heads, each compartment given its own ground colour and separated from its neighbours by a wide bar. What that does is shift the image from something beside the text to the text's own shape, so that reading is a visual act as well as a verbal one. The right response to the absence of portraits is therefore neither to call the book defective nor to suppose the text was secondary. This is a luxury object: purple and gold grounds, silver ink and dense ornament together are what a patron of rank can be shown, and the way to demonstrate that here is to make the letters themselves magnificent. The animal forms are the trap in this question, because a trained viewer reaches for the evangelist code, in which a winged man, a lion, an ox and an eagle stand for Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Inside a tiled initial those forms are part of a patterning with no narrative function, and a lion in a compartment of a letter is not Mark. The test to apply: ask what the decoration is attached to. Attached to the text, it is the argument for this book; placed in a separate picture, it would be an illustration; and a manuscript that has no pictures at all is not therefore a manuscript without an image.
questions.hint: Ask where the ornament sits relative to the text, and what a book with no pictures is still doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The registers of a Sanchi stupa gateway
questions.learningObjective: read a carved gateway as an ordered statement of a Buddhist cosmos
questions.stem: The torana, or carved gateway, at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, built between the first century BCE and the first century CE, carries three horizontal architraves stacked one above another, an elephant at each outer end of the topmost, and above the central pillar a wheel and a three-pronged emblem. What is the stacking of architraves and the pairing of animals doing?

options.text: Presenting the gateway as an ordered cosmos, with the animals and the emblems of the teaching at the top and narrative below
Showing that the gateway was rebuilt, since three courses can only be the record of three separate building campaigns
options.misconception: counts courses and infers campaigns, which nothing in a course count supports

options.text: Imitating a wooden gate, since stacking horizontal beams is a way of copying carpentry in stone
options.misconception: settles on a derivation from timber without evidence that the courses borrow anything

options.text: Making the structure lighter, since each course is set back from the one below and the load appears to decrease upwards
options.misconception: reads a symbolic programme as a structural device, when the courses are not working that way

questions.explanation: A gateway at a stupa is not primarily a door. It is a carved statement about what the monument encloses, and the statement is organised vertically. The elephants at the outer ends and the emblems above the central pillar, a wheel for the teaching itself and a three-pronged sign associated with the community that keeps it, sit at the top and the centre; below them run the narrative courses, and the lowest register carries the smallest and most numerous figures. Read that way, the gateway is doing three separate jobs at once. It gives the stupa an architectural face, so that the dome and the railing are announced at ground level to a visitor standing in front. It supplies a scale, because the courses are filled with figures of a known sort, from worshippers to gods, and a human figure is the only ruler in a set of symbols that would otherwise have no size at all. And it makes the enclosure legible as a sacred place before anyone enters it. The distractors each name a real property of a stacked course and then read it wrongly. Courses set back from one another do not lighten a stone gateway; the structure is a straight post carrying a straight beam, and the projection is a matter of cross-section, not of load. A count of three does not record three campaigns. And while stone does imitate timber elsewhere in the world, nothing about three courses establishes that, and a derivation claim needs evidence beyond the fact of resemblance. The gateway works because it is a diagram with figures in it, not because of anything it copies.
questions.hint: Ask what a course of small figures is for on a monument whose real content is a dome and a railing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The four hands of the Chola bronze of Shiva as Lord of Dance
questions.learningObjective: account for how a bronze encodes a sequence of acts in one standing figure
questions.stem: A Chola bronze of Shiva as Lord of Dance, cast in copper alloy and dated to about the late eleventh century, shows the god standing inside a ring of flame. His upper right hand carries a hand drum, his upper left hand holds a small flame, his lower right hand is raised with the palm outward, and his lower left foot is lifted while a small dwarf beneath the right foot twists away. The two raised hands alone would be a severe compositional problem. What resolves it?

options.text: A small number of copies, since a four-armed figure is only workable where a workshop held the same pattern unchanged
options.misconception: supposes a codified ensemble depends on workshop uniformity rather than on convention

options.text: The loss of the lower arms, since bronze cast in more than one pour often loses a projecting limb and leaves the pose tidier
options.misconception: explains a deliberate, balanced design as a casting loss that never occurred

options.text: A set of fixed attributes, since the ring of flame, the gestures and the objects are a codified system and the ensemble is read as a whole
The scale of the figure, since a small dwarf at the foot sets the size of the god and makes extra arms read as motion
options.misconception: attributes the readability of a multi-armed figure to relative scale, which does nothing for it

questions.explanation: Four arms is not a compositional problem in a tradition that has assigned an object and a gesture to each of them. What the ensemble records is a sequence: the drum that makes the first sound, the flame that will consume, the outward palm that allays fear, the pointed foot that offers refuge, and the dwarf of illusion pinned under the advancing foot. Each element is specified, and the specification is what makes the image legible. Because every element is fixed, the figure can be read at three levels at once, and viewers do read it at three levels. There is a narrative, in which creation and destruction happen and the god's foot tramples what misleads. There is a doctrinal reading, in which the same figure holds together the roles the tradition assigns to Shiva. And there is a bodily reading, in which the lifting of the left foot and the flying hair make the body a moving thing rather than a static column, which is why the bronze is not a support for the composition but the composition. Two of the wrong answers here are worth picking apart, because each names a real feature. A codified ensemble does not require a workshop that never varied the pattern, since copies in different metals and different sizes are exactly what a set of fixed attributes produces. And a dwarf at the foot is not there to measure anything; the ring of flame already supplies a measure, and the dwarf is there to be overcome. The bronze was also cast, not lost in a pour, and nothing about it suggests a missing limb.
questions.hint: Ask whether each hand and foot is specified, and what a reader gets from the combination.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The absence of a figure on the Book of Kells Chi Rho page
questions.learningObjective: explain an all-ornamental page as a decision about how a text is to be entered
questions.stem: On folio 34r of the Book of Kells, made about 800, the opening words of the Gospel of Matthew are written as enormous letters built from interlace, spirals, knots and cat and mouse forms, with a border of repeated creatures, and there is no human figure anywhere on the page. The same book does contain pictures of the evangelists elsewhere. What does the empty page at this point in the text do?

options.text: It makes entering the text an act of looking, since the letters themselves are the image and the reader must resolve the pattern to read
It marks the loss of an original, since a page at the opening of a Gospel would certainly have carried a picture of the author
options.misconception: assumes a missing picture, when a book full of pictures is plainly not short of them

options.text: It reserves the letters for the scribe and the ornament for another hand, since two different hands are visible in the page
options.misconception: converts a distribution of labour into an omission of a figure

options.text: It anticipates a change of subject, since a page with no figure prepares the reader for the narrative that follows
options.misconception: reads a decorative opening as foreshadowing a narrative, which it does not contain

questions.explanation: The right way to read this page is as a decision about how a reader begins. The first words of the Gospel are set out as a single field of interlace, and the field is organized so that a reader who knows the words sees them immediately and a reader who does not has to hunt for them inside a thicket of knots and spirals. The cat and mouse forms, the repeated border creatures and the abstracted human and animal heads embedded in the letters are not decoration around the text; they are what the text is made of. This is the opposite of the usual economy of an image, where a picture interprets a text quickly, and it changes the position of the reader from someone receiving a summary to someone doing work. The temptation in every direction is to supply a missing thing. It is tempting to say a picture of Matthew has been lost here, but the book is not short of pictures and this page is surrounded by them. It is tempting to see two hands, one for the letters and one for the pattern, but a book of this kind is a collaborative object throughout and nothing in the page marks a division. And it is tempting to read the page as preparation for a story, when the point of it is not narrative at all. The test to apply is functional: ask what the reader has to do here that they would not have to do on an ordinary text page. The answer is that they must look carefully, which is exactly the behaviour an opening page can ask for.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to do on this page that an ordinary page of text does not ask of them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The inhabited initial of the Lindisfarne Gospels incipit
questions.learningObjective: read a letter as a building containing figures
questions.stem: The incipit page to the Gospel of Matthew in the Lindisfarne Gospels, made about 715 to 720, shows a grid of interlace, knotwork and animals, and within one enormous initial there is a seated human figure, a bird, a man reaching for a book, and above them a winged man holding a book. Which feature of the page does the work of identifying the Gospel?

options.text: The winged man inside the letter, since the evangelist's own symbol settles who the following text is by, and it sits inside the structure of the text
The number of animals in the grid, since a fixed number belongs to each of the four evangelists
options.misconception: posits an arithmetic of animals per evangelist with nothing behind it

options.text: The knot pattern, since the tightness of the interlace records how early the book is and so dates the text it introduces
options.misconception: treats decorative complexity as a chronological index, which it is not

options.text: The colour of the ground behind the initial, since different evangelists are introduced on grounds of different hues
options.misconception: invents a colour code between evangelists that the page does not use

questions.explanation: The initial is doing the work of a frontispiece inside a letter. A winged man is the attribute attached to Matthew alone among the four evangelists, and a reader meeting it knows before reading a line who the following book is by. What makes the placement remarkable is that the figure is not placed beside the text but inside the structure of the text, occupying the bowl of the letter, so the identification is delivered in the form the reader is about to use. That is what inhabited initials do generally: they convert the opening of a book into a set of small pictures attached to the letters rather than to the page. The surrounding grid, with its interlace, its knotwork and its animals, is not a code and not a clock. There is no established link between a particular knot density and a particular date, so an argument that tightens from a knot pattern is arguing about a style and should be labelled as one. There is no colour code assigning a hue to each evangelist, and there is no fixed number of animals per evangelist. Both of those are the kind of detail a reader invents when a page is elaborate enough to seem systematic. The one thing to note about the beasts elsewhere on the page is that they are shown in conflict, in combat, or in the grip of an order, which is a statement about a world the manuscript imagines rather than an ornament to be decoded.
questions.hint: Ask which single attribute on the page belongs to one evangelist and to no other.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The uncoloured drawing of the Utrecht Psalter
questions.learningObjective: explain what a monochrome pen drawing is for in a working book
questions.stem: The Utrecht Psalter, made about 830 in a scriptorium that produced several books in the same manner, illustrates the whole text of the Psalms with pen drawing in brown ink on vellum, leaving the pages without colour and without gold. A second copy made in the same workshop about thirty years later repeats the same drawings almost exactly. What does that combination of features show the drawings were for?

options.text: A work of severe economy, since the absence of colour records a shortage of pigments in the scriptorium that produced them
options.misconception: reads a working method as a shortage, when the later copy is equally uncoloured

options.text: An early stage of a book that was never finished, since the pages were left ready for a colourist who never came
options.misconception: assumes an unfulfilled intention where two finished copies exist

options.text: A printed design, since a drawing that can be repeated exactly must have been traced from a printed model
options.misconception: confuses repeatability with print, when a pattern was traced from a pattern before it

options.text: Reproducible working copies, since a book of sketches could be traced and carried from workshop to workshop without any need to finish the pages

questions.explanation: These are the characteristics of a pattern book, and each of them points the same way. The drawing is in line rather than in colour, which means the whole design can be put down with one tool. The handling is quick and repetitive, so an entire psalm can be shown in a small number of consistent strokes. The book was made beside others in the same workshop in the same manner, which is what happens when a group of monks is being trained to draw. And the decisive evidence is the near copy: a second volume about thirty years later repeats the drawings so closely that the second was plainly traced from the first, or from a common exemplar. That is a working practice, not a finished state. The pattern was valuable because it could be carried and repeated, and repetition is exactly what a pattern is for. The two easy misreadings here are the ones that convert a method into an accident. A book with no colour is not evidence of a shortage, because the later copy has no colour either and was made by the same people in the same place. And an uncoloured book with two near-identical versions is not a book abandoned before finishing; it is a book that was never intended to be finished in that state. What the drawings lack is finish, and what they have is portability, which is the trade a workshop makes when it wants its designs to travel.
questions.hint: Ask what a second book that repeats the first book's drawings almost exactly is evidence of.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agitated line of the Ebbo Gospels evangelist portrait
questions.learningObjective: account for the relation between a copy and the energy of its line
questions.stem: In the Ebbo Gospels, made about 816 to 835 in the same city as the other surviving book of the group, the evangelist Matthew sits in a landscape, hunched forward, and every form is drawn with a thin, quick, repeatedly hooked line: the drapery, the hair, the frame of the chair, the small buildings behind him. The composition is closely based on a model shared with that other book. What is the relationship between the shared model and the changed line?

options.text: The line is the workshop's own, so the borrowed composition is retained and the handling is the part that differs
The line is unfinished, since a draft that is still being worked will be thin and hesitant in exactly this way
options.misconception: reads a consistent and deliberate line as hesitation and incompleteness

options.text: The line is a copy of the model's line, so a painter who altered the drawing would be contradicting his own exemplar
options.misconception: supposes fidelity to a model requires copying its handling as well as its layout

options.text: The line records a second attempt, since the same image was painted and then abandoned and begun again on the page
options.misconception: invents a lost first attempt to explain a deliberate style

questions.explanation: A model and a manner are two different things, and this book separates them cleanly. Its composition, the enthroned evangelist in a landscape with buildings behind, is shared with a related book produced in the same place and period, and that shared layout is what a workshop transmits: a way of arranging a subject that can be taught. The handling is not shared. The thin, hooked, repeatedly restarted line turns a solid drapery into a flicker of movement and gives a figure that is otherwise sitting still a nervous energy, and that is local to this book. The two claims about the line are worth separating. A model is not a tracing, because a workshop that reproduces a model's line reproduces the model rather than adding anything, and a book in which the drawing is the point would have nothing to contribute. Nor is a quick line an incomplete one. Hesitation leaves marks that wander and thin out; a deliberate line can be uniform in weight and still be fast, and here every form is built from the same hooked stroke, which is a learned manner rather than an abandoned attempt. The useful generalisation is that a workshop transmits composition readily and handling reluctantly, and that the second is what most usefully identifies a hand. A shared layout is evidence of contact; a different line is evidence of a different decision about how a figure should move.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the page a workshop passes on and which part a painter decides for himself.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The Coronation Gospels as a pledge object
questions.learningObjective: connect the physical make of a book to the political rite it was used in
questions.stem: A Gospel book made at the court of Charlemagne between about 794 and 800, now in the imperial treasury in Vienna, is the volume that a later emperor is said to have placed under his hand at a coronation while swearing an oath, with his fingers resting on the page of John's Gospel. It has four evangelist portraits, sixteen plates of precious metal, and a jewelled cover. What do the material facts and the use together tell you about the book?

options.text: That its value is documentary, since a book named in a coronation oath fixes the date of the ceremony exactly
options.misconception: treats a tradition about a rite as if it fixed a ceremony to a year

options.text: That it was built to be handled in a public rite, so the text inside is a pledge and the object itself is what makes the pledge binding
That it was a private reading book, since the precious cover and the portraits show it was made for one person's devotion
options.misconception: reads sumptuousness as private rather than as public display

options.text: That it was made to be looked at rather than read, since the plates and the cover leave no room for the text on an opening
options.misconception: assumes metal plates and a jewel case prevent a book being opened and read

questions.explanation: The most productive way to look at this book is to ask what it had to do, and then to check the physical facts against the answer. It had to be carried into a public ceremony, opened, held flat by one hand, and shown to an assembly. A jewelled cover and sixteen plates of precious metal are not decoration added to a devotional volume; they are what makes the volume equal in weight and worth to the parties to a political act, so that a dispute about the oath is a dispute about the object itself. That is why the cover can be later than the book, and why a treasure like this survives in a treasury rather than in a library: it was accumulated as a pledge, not shelved as a text. The failure modes in the distractors are each a plausible habit. Sumptuousness is regularly read as private, but a court that buys gold plate for a book is buying something to be seen, and a private chapel needs no precious metal. A cover does not stop a book from being opened, which is exactly what the oath requires. And a tradition about which book was used is not a dated record of a ceremony; the book's own colophon and the shape of its text carry the datable evidence, and the ceremony is a later association. The conclusion is a general one: a book's use tells you what its expense was for, and here the answer is a public act with the text as its instrument.
questions.hint: Ask what the object has to be able to do when it is placed under a hand in front of an assembly.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The painted and gilded surface of the Gero Crucifix
questions.learningObjective: describe how a carved figure is finished to produce a specific effect on the viewer
questions.stem: A wooden crucifix made about 970 for Cologne Cathedral, in oak with a surface of painted and gilded detail, shows Christ with his eyes open, his head fallen back, his body sagging at the waist while the arms still pull upward, and blood running from the wound in the side down across the loincloth. What is the figure designed to make happen in front of a viewer standing below it?

options.text: That the body strains against what holds it, so the conflict between the sagging torso and the raised arms is the event the surface records
That the figure is small enough to be carried, so the carved core was made to be held and the detail was added for close viewing
options.misconception: infers a portable scale from the fineness of a painted surface

options.text: That the surface has been restored, since a gold loincloth and painted blood are typical of a later campaign on an old panel
options.misconception: assigns a later date from the presence of colour and gold alone

options.text: That the figure is a corpse, so the open eyes and the running blood are the painter's corrections to make a dead Christ look alive
options.misconception: reads the strain as a technical correction of a dead body rather than as its subject

questions.explanation: The carving is built around a contradiction, and the contradiction is the subject. The arms are drawn upward by the nails, so the shoulders rise and the chest lifts, but the waist drops and the knees bend the other way, so the body hangs. A figure constructed in that way does not look at rest and does not look like a corpse; it looks like something being pulled in two directions, and a viewer standing below sees the effort before the wound. The surface finish then does work that a bare carving could not. The open eyes with their reddened whites, the blood laid in a wet line from the side wound, the gold of the loincloth and the punched and painted pattern that sits on top of the wood are all close-range marks, made for a viewer at a distance of a few feet and in a dim interior, and they concentrate attention on the body rather than on the cross. A close study of the carving finds the body first and the detail later, which is the right order for a devotional object. Two errors are worth naming because they are common. The strain is not a painter correcting a dead body, since a corpse hangs and does not fight; the open eyes and the blood belong to a living Christ in the instant of dying. And colour and gold are original to this class of object, not evidence of a later hand, because a carved and painted surface was the norm for a tenth-century crucifix, not a repair. The test to apply: describe the pose as a sculptor would, and see whether the description already contains the meaning.
questions.hint: Ask whether the arms and the waist are pulling the same way or in opposite directions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The enthroned emperor in the Gospels of Otto III
questions.learningObjective: account for scale and crowd as a statement of authority in a book of hours' size
questions.stem: In a Gospel book made about 1000, one of a group of sumptuous books from the same scriptorium, a double page shows an emperor enthroned inside a domed building, larger than the figures who flank him, while figures representing the provinces of the realm come forward carrying gifts. The other pages carry the four evangelists and a long cycle of scenes. Which page does the work's argument rest on?

options.text: On the evangelist cycle, since the biblical scenes are the only part of a Gospel book that carries meaning of its own
options.misconception: asserts that the text pages are meaningless while an image page is not

options.text: On neither, since a Gospel book is a liturgical object whose images are decoration and whose meaning lies wholly in the text
options.misconception: reduces an illustrated codex to a decorated text and denies that images can carry argument

options.text: On the cover, since the jewelled binding is what a viewer saw first and the pages are what a viewer read
options.misconception: puts the argument in a cover that was made later than the book inside it

options.text: On the enthronement page, since the presentation of the empire to the ruler is the theme the whole book is built to carry

questions.explanation: The composition tells you what the book is for. An emperor enthroned in architecture, drawn larger than the other figures, receiving the gifts of the provinces, is a statement about who holds the empire, and the fact that it takes a double page says it is the statement the book was made to make. The rest of the book is what such an object needs: the text of the Gospels, four evangelist portraits, and a cycle of scenes that lets the text be entered through pictures. The scale difference is not a defect of proportion. Hierarchy of size is a normal means in this kind of imagery, and the buildings in the background are not there to correct it but to supply a setting appropriate to a ruler. Three wrong readings are available and all are worth rejecting explicitly. First, that the biblical cycle is the only meaningful content, which assumes images have no argument in a codex; the whole page described is an image and it argues. Second, that a Gospel book is only a text, which mistakes a liturgical function for a claim about meaning; a book read aloud in a chapel is exactly the kind of object that gets a cycle of scenes. Third, that the cover carries the argument, which inverts the chronology: a treasure binding of this kind was normally made later, and the binding follows the value the pages had already acquired rather than the other way round. The test to apply: ask which page an owner would want shown, and to whom.
questions.hint: Ask which page the patron would want seen, and which the later binding was made to fit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The flattened ground of the Bamberg Apocalypse
questions.learningObjective: explain how a metal ground can carry light without carrying space
questions.stem: In the Bamberg Apocalypse, made about 1000 to 1020, the pages have a ground of gold and silver laid over vellum, and the figures are drawn with hard, calligraphic contour lines that then break into angular folds. A seated figure's drapery is a series of zigzags that do not describe a body beneath, and the ground behind is untested and unmodulated. What does the combination of ground and line produce?

options.text: An influence from Byzantine metalwork, since angular drapery folds are only ever a borrowing from worked silver
options.misconception: reduces a drawing convention to a derivation from one material

options.text: A damaged book, since a ground of gold and silver would oxidise and the untested areas are where it has gone
options.misconception: reads an intact, deliberately flat ground as chemical loss

options.text: A surface on which the figure exists as an event rather than as a body in a place, since the ground denies space and the line supplies the energy
A stage in the process, since the outlines were drawn first and the modelling was intended and abandoned
options.misconception: assumes an abandoned modelling step where the flatness is the design

questions.explanation: Two flat surfaces, one behind and one on the figure, and together they produce a very specific effect. The ground is an unmodulated field of precious metal, so it holds no light, no shadow and no distance; it is simply the limit of the page. On that field, the contour line does the whole job, and it is a contour line that keeps breaking into angular folds, so a seated body becomes a rhythm of zigzags that is legible as drapery without ever settling into a described mass. What the page has then is a figure that is present in full and located nowhere. This is a way of showing an action, of showing the angel at the side of a throne or a figure in the act of receiving a book, and the emphasis falls on the energy of the line rather than on the weight of the body. The distractors all turn a design decision into an accident or a borrowing. Gold and silver ground on vellum was normal and durable, so an even field is not a loss. Angular folds are a drawing convention used across Europe in this period and are not the property of worked silver. And a flat ground with sharp contour is not a half-finished modelling job, since there is no modelled area anywhere that could be read as an abandoned step. The practical test: ask what the light is doing on the page. Here it is doing almost nothing, and that is the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the ground supplies, and then ask what is left for the outline to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The dated signature on the Stavelot Triptych
questions.learningObjective: use a signature and a style together without confusing them
questions.stem: A triptych of oak panels covered with gold and silver leaf, painted and fitted with relief silverwork, carries an inscription in Latin giving the year 1094. Its figures are tall, thin and swaying, with long curved lines, large hands and small heads, and they are set on a gold ground with drapery worked in fine parallel strokes. It was made for a Benedictine abbey in the Meuse region. Which statement about this object is properly supported?

options.text: Neither statement is usable, since an inscription can be copied and a style can be learned, so both kinds of evidence fail
options.misconception: draws a false equivalence between fallible and useless, which empties the object of information

options.text: The inscription dates the commission, and the style locates the workshop's sources, and neither settles the other on its own
The inscription proves the work was finished in 1094, since a maker who signs a date does not vary it
options.misconception: takes a date on an object as a guarantee about the moment the paint was applied

options.text: The style proves the work was made in Byzantium, since only a Byzantine workshop produced gold grounds of that quality
options.misconception: infers a place of production from a ground that was used widely

questions.explanation: Two kinds of evidence are doing different work, and the correct use of them is to keep them apart. The inscription is a documentary act, and a dated signature tells you what the commissioning party recorded, which in a monastic context is normally the date of the contract or of the dedication rather than the hour the last gold leaf was burnished. It is a strong piece of evidence and it has a proper use: it fixes the object in time. The style is a different kind of evidence and it answers a different question. Tall thin swaying figures, large hands, small heads, and drapery in fine parallel strokes are a set of characteristics that a workshop in the Meuse region could learn and did learn from sources to the south and east, which is why a gold ground in northern Europe is not a production site. The three failures in the distractors are each a common overreach. A signature is not a guarantee about the minute of execution, and it can in principle be copied, which is a reason to test it rather than a reason to discard it. A shared convention is not a shared workshop. And the claim that both kinds of evidence are useless commits the opposite error to credulity: an inscription and a stylistic comparison each carry real weight, they simply carry it on separate questions, and an attribution built from both is stronger than one built from either.
questions.hint: Ask what each kind of evidence is competent to establish, and keep the two questions apart.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The written captions of the Bayeux Embroidery
questions.learningObjective: account for a text that comments on the pictures it accompanies
questions.stem: The Bayeux Embroidery, worked in wool on linen about the 1070s, tells a campaign in a single band about fifty centimetres high, and above or below the figures are short written statements in Latin. Some name the people shown. Others comment: one reads in effect, and another, HIC ODO EPISCOPUS BACULUM TENENS CONFORTAT PUEROS, names the bishop with his club encouraging the boys. What do those commentating captions do that the figures do not?

options.text: They supply a voice, since the figures carry the action and the words attribute intention, rank and response to it
They identify the embroiderer, since a signature is always hidden in a written band on a work of this kind
options.misconception: reads any writing on a textile as a maker's signature

options.text: They supply error, since a text attached to a picture must be inaccurate where the picture is clear
options.misconception: assumes words and images inevitably disagree, which is not what a discrepancy would show

options.text: They record measurements, since a written label beside a figure fixes the length of the ships and the height of the tower
options.misconception: supplies numbers the captions do not contain

questions.explanation: The embroidery's problem is that wool thread cannot do what a text does, and the captions solve exactly that problem. A figure can be shown holding a club and standing among other men, and nothing in the gesture says that the club is episcopal, that the men are children, or that the gesture means encouragement. The caption converts an image into an account: it names the rank of a man, it supplies the motive, and it lets a reader who cannot see the band follow the argument. That is why some captions name and others comment, and why the commenting ones matter more to the work. It also explains the whole structure of the piece. In a long band, roughly the height of a standing adult, figures are crowded, faces are shown in profile and three-quarter view, and several events have to share the ground. A caption is a way of sequencing a narrative that pictures alone would flatten into a single scene. The three wrong answers here are all invented functions. There are no measurements in the captions, and none of the written statements gives a dimension. Where words and images do disagree, and in this embroidery they sometimes do about who did what and when, the disagreement is informative about the point of view, not a defect in the technique. And a band of writing running the length of a work is a narrative apparatus, not a signature; nothing in the captions names a maker.
questions.hint: Ask what a gesture can show and what it cannot, and which of those the caption supplies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The viewpoint of a lamentation in the Arena Chapel, Padua
questions.learningObjective: read a crowd of figures as a set of different viewing positions
questions.stem: In the Lamentation painted about 1305 on the wall of the Scrovegni, or Arena, Chapel in Padua, the dead Christ lies on a broken ledge at the bottom of a rocky cleft, and about ten figures stand around him. Several are shown from behind, kneeling or bending, and one face is turned sharply upward, away from the body. What is the arrangement of the group doing that a single viewpoint could not?

options.text: It is showing a crowd caught at random, since the painters of this period took figures from whatever poses were convenient
options.misconception: reads deliberate viewpoint as indifferent selection

options.text: It is copying a crowd from a real event, since the number of mourners is a record of how many attended a funeral
options.misconception: treats a figure count as a documentary tally of an event

options.text: It is building depth, since figures seen from behind necessarily stand behind the figures seen from the front
options.misconception: conflates showing where a figure stands with showing how far away it is

options.text: It is presenting several places to stand at once, so the viewer can be kneeling in the crowd, standing behind it, or looking up as the figure at the rear does

questions.explanation: A wall painting is read from one place, but the group around the body is not arranged as if it were seen from one place. Figures are shown from behind, from the side, kneeling, and one turns the face up and away. Each of those is a different position a viewer could occupy, and the painter is offering all of them in one image. This is the decisive difference between this kind of wall painting and a stage set, where every figure is aligned to a single spectator. The rock cleft is doing related work. It gives a hard diagonal that runs from high on one side down to the body, so the eye is delivered to the lowest point in the composition, and it provides a floor that is above and beside the figures rather than a continuous ground they all share. The figures are therefore stacked rather than ranged, which is what lets so many of them be present at once. The three errors here are all cases of reading a formal decision as something else. A crowd is composed; the poses are chosen so that the eye has somewhere to be. The number of mourners is a matter of space on the wall, not a tally of an attendance. And showing a figure from behind does not by itself establish depth: it establishes where that figure is standing, and the difference matters, because the painting is not primarily about a measurable recession any more than a mosaic is. The test: ask, of each figure, where a person would have to stand to see it as drawn. The answers differ, and that is the point.
questions.hint: Ask where a person would have to stand to see each figure the way it is drawn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Perspective relief on a bronze door panel
questions.learningObjective: account for depth that is graded rather than measured
questions.stem: A gilded bronze door panel cast between 1425 and 1452 for a Baptistery in Florence shows a flagellation, with the main action set in a deep, cut-back architecture whose lines converge, and figures standing on a pavement whose squares diminish steadily toward the back. The relief is deepest at the front and nearly flat at the rear. What is the device doing that a painted surface would do differently?

options.text: Foreshortening the whole panel, so the door is intended to be seen at an angle rather than square from the front
options.misconception: confuses a device inside the relief with the viewing angle of the door itself

options.text: Saving metal, since a shallow rear is cheaper to cast than a deep one and explains the design economically
options.misconception: offers a cost reason where a formal reason is available and stated in the panel

options.text: Reproducing a painting, since a door panel of this kind was always cast from a design supplied by a painter
options.misconception: supposes the bronze must be after a painting rather than a drawing

options.text: Grading the depth of the relief to match the depth of the space, so the relief is a measured gradient rather than a picture of a gradient

questions.explanation: The panel solves a problem that a painting solves with a flat mark. A painted surface can describe a recession by making a line thinner or a colour paler, but it has no depth to give away. A cast panel has real depth to spend, and the way to spend it is to make the relief shallow exactly where the described space is far away. Deep at the front, shallow at the back, the physical profile of the metal and the implied profile of the architecture run together, so the two reinforce each other instead of fighting. That is why the pavement works here. The squares of a paved floor are the plainest possible way of saying how far back something is, and on a door they have a second advantage: they are the same kind of measurable grid that a painted floor uses, so the panel is arguing for a space that can be checked. The convergence of the architectural lines points the same way. Note what the device is not. It is not about the door being viewed at an angle, since a door is a frontal object and the panel is composed for a viewer standing square in front of it. It is not about saving metal, though a shallow rear is cheaper; the front of this panel is deep enough that casting it was the difficult part, and the gradient is arranged for what the eye needs. And the design does not need to be after a painting: a drawing carries the same scheme, and the foundry works from a pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what a cast surface can do that a painted surface cannot, and where the depth is deepest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stance of the bronze David in Florence
questions.learningObjective: relate the weight distribution of a standing figure to the viewer's position
questions.stem: A bronze David cast about the 1440s for the courtyard of a Florentine palace and now in the Museo Nazionale del Bargello stands about 1.5 metres high. The weight rests almost entirely on one leg, the other leg bent and drawn back with the toe just touching the ground, and the head turns sharply to the left with the brows drawn. What does the distribution of weight do for a viewer standing in front of it?

options.text: It makes the figure occupy a shallow space, so the twist and the bent leg read as movement that crosses the space in front of the viewer
It places the figure in a landscape, since a contrapposto stance is only meaningful against a horizon and a ground line
options.misconception: supposes the pose depends on a background that the bronze does not have

options.text: It makes the figure look unfinished, since a leg that touches the ground only at the toe leaves the cast ambiguous
options.misconception: treats a deliberate and legible stance as an unresolved casting problem

options.text: It makes the figure appear heavy, since a stance that puts all the weight on one leg is the way a body is drawn when it is about to fall
options.misconception: reads a balanced standing pose as the sign of a collapse

questions.explanation: A standing bronze with one leg free is not a design problem but a solution to one. If the whole weight sat on both legs the figure would be a column: it would hold a position indefinitely and it would face the viewer square. Putting the weight on one leg and letting the other leg swing free gives the body a slight spiral, from the turned foot through the hip and shoulder to the turned head, and that spiral needs depth to happen in. The figure therefore occupies a shallow box and moves within it, and a viewer has to move a little to follow the twist. The toe just touching the ground is doing real work, because it is what makes the free leg read as a decision rather than as a loss of balance, and it is why the pose is legible as poise and not as collapse. The face sharpens the effect: the brows are drawn and the head is turned away from the direction the body advances, so the figure is not simply walking anywhere. Three errors to clear away. A single-leg stance is the classic statement of ease, not of falling. A free leg that touches lightly is a controlled outcome, not an ambiguous casting, and the figure is finished and finished with care. And the pose works with no landscape at all, which is exactly what a free-standing figure for a courtyard needs: a bronze that depended on a horizon could not be carried around or set anywhere. The test: ask what the space between the two legs is for. Here it is a volume the eye travels through.
questions.hint: Ask what a single supporting leg lets the rest of the body do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The ground plane of the Pisanello Saint George fresco
questions.learningObjective: explain the cost of a composition with no continuous ground
questions.stem: In the fresco of Saint George and the Princess painted about 1435 to 1440 in Sant'Anastasia, Verona, the saint on a rearing horse and a dragon fill a tall, narrow wall, with an unpainted area above and a broken strap and a date on a slip of paper painted on the wall itself. The horse has no ground under its feet and the princess and her retinue stand in a different, flatter band. What does the missing ground do to the scene?

options.text: It flattens the picture, since figures without a ground have no relation to one another and so cannot be compared in depth
options.misconception: supposes overlapping figures cannot establish a depth order

options.text: It makes the action hang, so the encounter reads as an event suspended rather than as a place the figures occupy together
It shows the wall is unfinished, since a fresco with no ground line was simply never completed at the bottom
options.misconception: reads a compositional choice as unfinished work at the base of the wall

options.text: It identifies the painter, since only a painter trained in one centre omits a ground line in this particular way
options.misconception: uses a single compositional habit to name a hand without any comparison

questions.explanation: The absence of a ground line is the organising fact of this fresco, and it has to be read as a decision with a cost. Where several figures occupy a shared ground, the eye is given a floor to measure against and a horizon to measure down from, and the result is a space that is more or less continuous. Here the ground is broken, and because it is broken the figures belong to different orders rather than to one place. The horse and the dragon are the encounter, and they are drawn to fill the shape they are in. The princess and her retinue occupy a band that is flatter and quieter, as though the spectacle is being watched from a place outside it. The painted strap and the dated slip on the wall work the same way, pulling a piece of everyday material up into the field of the action. The three errors here are all attempts to make a compositional decision mean something safer. A missing ground is not a missing painting; frescoes in this position are frequently designed to the shape of the wall, and the area above is often simply left. Nor does one habit identify a painter, since the same omission can be a habit of a workshop, a taste, or a solution to a narrow field. And the claim that a figure without ground cannot be compared in depth is simply false, because overlapping and relative scale order figures very well without a floor; that is how this fresco is legible at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a floor gives the eye that overlapping and scale do not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirror and the joined inscription in the Arnolfini Portrait
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a mirror records from what it seems to record
questions.stem: A painting of a man and a woman in a room, made in 1434 by Jan van Eyck and now in the National Gallery, London, shows a small convex mirror on the back wall between two windows. Its frame carries ten small scenes around its edge, and in its surface two figures appear in the doorway with their backs turned, one of them red. What is the mirror doing that a flat mirror or a plain window could not?

options.text: Attesting to the marriage, since the joined hands and the two figures reflected are a sworn act and the glass records it
options.misconception: supplies a legal conclusion the reflection cannot establish

options.text: Fixing the time of the scene, since a mirror reflects whatever is before it at that instant and so dates the occasion
options.misconception: treats a reflection as a timestamp, when it shows position rather than time

options.text: Extending the space behind the picture, so the room is shown to continue past the front the viewer faces, with the picture's own surface inside it
Reducing the room, since a curved surface compresses what it shows and makes a small chamber look larger than it is
options.misconception: claims a convex surface enlarges what it reflects, which is the opposite of what it does

questions.explanation: A convex mirror is an instrument of extension, and that is exactly what this one is doing. The room is drawn in one-point perspective toward a back wall, and into that wall the painter has set a small glass that shows two people standing in a doorway, seen from behind, at the very place where the viewer is standing. So the picture contains its own front. The two reflected figures are part of the room's depth and also, whatever else they are, occupants of the space between the picture and the person looking at it, and that is a problem a flat mirror could not pose because a flat mirror shows a space in front of itself rather than a space that contains it. The small scenes around the frame, which show episodes of the Passion, add a second function: the object is not only a lens but a piece of imported or attributed meaning. Three claims need rejecting. The mirror does not fix a time. A reflection records a position relative to the mirror, and a painting of one does not become a snapshot by containing one. Nor does it attest a marriage; a great deal of argument about the subject of this picture has turned on whether it is a marriage, a betrothal, a legal contract, or a memorial, and the mirror has been read as evidence for more than one of those. And a convex surface reduces what it shows, which is why the two figures are small; the room is not enlarged, it is extended.
questions.hint: Ask where the reflected figures are standing relative to the viewer, not relative to the wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The intrusion of the angel in the Merode Altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: read a domestic object as carrying a figure in a narrative
questions.stem: A triptych of about 1427 to 1432, in oak, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, shows an angel entering a workshop room through an opening in the wall, with one knee already through, while a young woman in a red dress at a bench has turned and dropped the jug she was holding. On the sill stands a small wooden trap with a mousetrap and a dead bird on it, and lilies stand in a jug on the same table. What is the significance of the angel's position, given the props?

options.text: The angel is a later addition, since a figure caught mid-entry is a shape that a painter of this period could not draw
options.misconception: supposes a motif is beyond a painter's reach and therefore a later hand

options.text: The room is the main subject, since the workshop furniture fills most of the panel and the figure is small within it
options.misconception: lets the quantity of domestic detail outrank the narrative moment in the panel

options.text: The vessels are inventory, since a triptych of this kind lists the goods a household owned at that date
options.misconception: reads the objects as a record of ownership rather than as a set of signs

options.text: The message has already arrived, so the scene sits between two moments, and the objects on the sill carry a further reading of it

questions.explanation: The position of the angel is a decision about time, and it is the kind of decision a painter makes in order to put two moments in one picture. The angel is not arriving, because the young woman has already turned and the jug has already gone down; the message has landed. The scene is therefore the instant after, and everything in the room is a reading of the instant before. That is what the props on the sill are for. A small wooden trap with a baited cup and a dead bird beside it, together with lilies standing in a jug, is a cluster of images that has been much argued over and that includes a suggestion of entrapment and a sign of purity, and they work only because the viewer has grasped that something has just happened. The careful hand at the kettle and the washing towel hung on a rod complete a household caught out in the middle of a day. The three failures are all ways of discounting the figure. A motif of interrupted entry is well within this painter's range, since he draws a knee through an opening and a stopped jug as readily as a wing. The size of the room relative to the figure is a matter of the subject, and the subject of this panel is a message arriving, not an interior. And the objects are not a list: a list would not include a trap set on a sill beside a dead bird, which is a sign and not a possession.
questions.hint: Ask whether the angel is arriving or has already arrived, and what the viewer sees that tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The compressed box of the Descent from the Cross
questions.learningObjective: explain a shallow space built for figures rather than for landscape
questions.stem: A panel painted about 1435 and now in the Prado shows the body of Christ being lowered from the cross inside a shallow gold-backed niche, with about ten figures packed into a compartment barely wider than the group. A swooning figure in blue is held up at the right, the ladder stands in front, and the horizon is high. What does the compression produce?

options.text: A space governed by the group, since the depth available is set by the figures and the background closes in behind them
A private devotional object, since a panel too small for a chapel can only have been made for a person to hold
options.misconception: infers a use from a size and a format alone

options.text: A distant setting, since a high horizon with no landscape is the standard way of signalling far-off country
options.misconception: reads the absence of landscape as a sign of distance rather than of a closed ground

options.text: A space too small to hold the event, since a body being lowered needs more room than a painted niche can show
options.misconception: treats a shallow box as a failure to fit the subject

questions.explanation: A shallow compartment like this one is built to a specification, and the specification is the group. The figures are large in relation to the field, they overlap in layers, and the back of the niche closes at a distance measured in a body length rather than in a landscape. Depth is therefore available in small amounts and spent where the narrative needs it: the ladder stands in front so that the action of the descent is legible, the body of Christ lies across the horizontal of the tomb, and the space that opens is the space the arms of the cross and the reaching figures occupy. The high horizon is part of the same economy, since it puts the ground close under the figures and leaves the upper field for the gold. The gold-backed niche is not a failure to paint a setting. It is a declaration about what kind of space is being offered, and a gold ground in a panel of this period means that the scene is presented rather than located. Three claims need clearing away. A cramped space is not an incompetent fit; the compression is what makes ten figures readable at all. A high horizon with no landscape does not mean the country is far away, it means there is no country. And the size of a panel does not determine its use: altarpieces with shutters carry precisely this kind of image, and a work of this class was made for a church.
questions.hint: Ask what sets the scale of the depth, and whether the figures or the landscape do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The closed wings of the Ghent Altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: describe how a hinged altarpiece controls a viewer's encounter
questions.stem: A triptych painted in 1432 for a church in Ghent, twelve painted panels on one hinged frame, is a very large object: when the wings are open it spans roughly 4.7 metres. On the outer faces, when it is shut, the two donors stand beside their patron saints in a shallow loggia, and the inner faces of two of those panels are painted in grey with two standing figures of saints. What does the shut state do that a fixed altarpiece cannot?

options.text: It removes the donors, since a commission wants the object to be read and the patrons to be forgotten once the payment is made
options.misconception: supplies a motive the donor portraits on the outer wings directly contradict

options.text: It makes the reading conditional, so what a visitor sees is a sequence of states that the object itself controls
It protects the paint, since a closed frame shields the interior from light and air and so preserves the colours beneath
options.misconception: supplies a conservation motive where the outer panels carry a donor portrait

options.text: It doubles the value, since every additional surface is another painted area and the commission was priced by the panel
options.misconception: assumes commissions were costed by surface area rather than by agreed terms

questions.explanation: A hinged altarpiece is a device for sequencing, and its outer surface is a designed state rather than a cover. Shut, the visitor meets a pair of donors with their patron saints in a shallow architectural setting, presented at a scale and in a frame that fits the wall it stands on; the grey inner faces of two of the outer panels, painted to look like sculpture, mark the point at which one state gives way to the other. Open, the object becomes a picture about 4.7 metres wide and the experience is of a different order entirely, and the wide Adoration at the centre of the inner face is the panel everything else is arranged around. So the object does not present one image but a set of states that a viewer, a priest, or a visiting dignitary controls by opening and closing it. That is a different relationship between work and viewer from a fixed altarpiece, and it is why the grey imitation sculpture matters: it announces a change of register at the threshold. The three wrong answers each attribute a motive that the object does not support. The outer wings carry a donor portrait, so the shut state is not a protective measure. A commission was agreed as a whole and the contract, not the panel count, set the price. And a patron who is painted on the outside with his patron saint is plainly not asking to be forgotten.
questions.hint: Ask what a visitor is shown first, and what the hinges make possible that a fixed panel does not.
