questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The single vanishing point of the Tribute Money fresco
questions.learningObjective: account for a unified light and eye level in a wall painting
questions.stem: A fresco painted about 1425 to 1427 in a chapel in Florence shows a tax collector, an apostle, Christ and a crowd, set against a painted building whose receding lines meet at a single point, at a height that puts the vanishing point at about eye level for a person standing on the chapel floor. The light on the faces and on the rock comes from one direction. Which of these details is doing the most work?

options.text: The painted building, because a building is the only object in the fresco that can establish a direction of recession at all
options.misconception: claims architecture is the only source of a recession cue, when overlap and scale also supply one

options.text: The single light source, because one light is what makes a scene look like a single moment rather than a set of scenes
options.misconception: gives the light credit for a job the geometry is doing

options.text: The eye-level vanishing point, because it fixes where the chapel's own floor puts the viewer and so ties the painted space to the standing body
The crowd, since a number of figures at different depths is the only way to show that a scene takes place over time
options.misconception: treats a figure group as a time scale rather than a spatial one

questions.explanation: The building is the instrument, but the vanishing point is the point. A single point at which receding lines converge, set at the height of a standing person's eye, does two things at once. It establishes one consistent space rather than several, so the figures at different distances share a world, and it fixes the height of the horizon at the level of a real observer. On a chapel wall that second effect is decisive, because it means the painted room is a continuation of the room the congregation is standing in, at the level of their own heads. A construction that had put the vanishing point high or low would announce itself as a picture of a space seen from somewhere other than here, and the wall would cease to be a window. The light is working too, and it is worth being precise about what: one consistent source means the modelling in the picture agrees with itself, so the figures and the rock are lit as one event. But that is a coherence, and coherence is a lesser achievement than the tying of the painted space to the actual floor. The distractors each promote one true detail into the decisive one. A building is not the only source of a recession cue, since overlapping and diminishing scale do the same work. A crowd does not measure time; the sequence in which the scene is read does, and the crowd measures distance. And a single light makes an image consistent rather than making it continuous with a real room.
questions.hint: Ask which measurement is made from the floor the congregation is standing on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three figures in the Baptism of Christ
questions.learningObjective: explain a composition held in a strict geometric order
questions.stem: A panel painted in egg tempera on poplar about 1445 to 1450, now in the National Gallery, London, shows Christ standing waist-deep in a river between two banks, an angel holding his garment on the right bank, and three angels on the left bank. The banks are curved, the third angel's head sits on the horizon, and the whole arrangement is built from a few arcs. What is the composition's governing idea?

options.text: A narrative sequence, since three angels and two banks stand for the three moments by which the event is unfolded
options.misconception: invents a three-moment sequence where the panel shows one moment

options.text: A portrait group, since the two flanking figures are the donor and his wife and their likenesses are specific
options.misconception: assigns portrait likenesses without evidence of patron and sitter

options.text: A landscape study, since the river and the banks are painted with more care than the figures and the setting is the subject
options.misconception: reverses the emphasis of a panel whose figures hold the composition

options.text: A measured order, since the figures and the arcs are placed so that the panel's geometry holds the group in exact balance

questions.explanation: The panel is built the way a treatise builds an argument, and the building is the subject. The river is a shallow curve, the banks are arcs struck from centres that fall within the panel, the heads of the figures fall at measured heights, and one angel's head is placed so that it sits on the horizon. The result is a group in which nothing is arbitrary, and the eye is given no loose end to follow. What that buys is worth stating, because it is the point of the picture. The event is one of immersion, risk and transition, and a composition built on measured arcs holds Christ exactly between two banks: not yet on the far side, not yet out of the water. The gesture of the third angel, whose hand points at the second, is placed so that the line it makes is part of the geometry rather than an event laid on top of it. The three wrong readings are all additions. Nothing in the panel unfolds in time; the three angels are simultaneous, and a repetition is not a sequence. Nothing identifies the flanking figures as a married couple, and their clothes belong to no recognisable portrait type. And the setting is the servant of the subject, not its master: the river is painted carefully because the geometry needs it, and the figures need the geometry. The test to apply: measure the panel. If the significant points fall on arcs and on a horizon line, the composition is a construction, and the construction is the argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the arcs and the horizon are for, and try to measure where the significant points fall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The receding street of the Crivelli Annunciation
questions.learningObjective: identify a single vanishing point used for a religious event in a town street
questions.stem: A panel dated 1486 and now in the National Gallery, London, shows an annunciation in a town. The Gabriel stands in a street at the left in a foreshortened loggia, the Mary is at the right in front of a plain wall, and between them the street recedes sharply, its roof lines and the courses of the paving converging on a single point well below the horizon. A peacock stands in the garden and an apple lies on the parapet. What has the painter used the street to do?

options.text: To make a measurable depth between two events that a flatter composition would have held at the same distance
To explain the apple, since a fruit lying on a parapet in a receding street is a device for showing a fall
options.misconception: fixes on a single object and invents a narrative it is not part of

options.text: To put the angel outside the event, since a figure drawn in perspective is by definition at a distance from the viewer
options.misconception: confuses a figure's placement in a drawn space with its distance from a spectator

options.text: To give the town a date, since tiled roofs and paved courses belong to one century and not to another
options.misconception: treats a rendered street as a dated document rather than as a constructed space

questions.explanation: Two events, at the left and at the right of the panel, have to be felt as happening at the same time and in the same world. A flat composition would place them side by side and nothing more. The street is what joins them, because it establishes a measurable interval: the roof lines and the courses of the paving converge, and the interval between the two figures can be read off that convergence. The point of convergence sits below the horizon, which is what makes the view look down a street rather than across a plain, and it is also what keeps the two sides of the panel from being symmetrical neighbours. Everything else in the painting plays on the same measured world. The peacock and the cut apple on the parapet sit on the same line that establishes the depth, so they are part of the geometry rather than a still life that has been inserted. Three errors need clearing away. A rendered town is not a dated document; roofs and paving were available to a painter for a career. Being drawn in a space does not put a figure away from the viewer, since perspective concerns the position of figures relative to one another and to a vanishing point. And the apple is not there to demonstrate gravity or a fall; it is a sign, and its job is to sit on the line that measures the interval. The test: ask which of the objects on the parapet would have to be moved if the depth were wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the interval between the angel and the Mary has to be, and how the street supplies it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A gold ground inside a rendered room
questions.learningObjective: explain how two conventions coexist in one small panel
questions.stem: A small panel painted in tempera about 1480, now in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli in Milan, shows a seated woman reading with a child on her knees, in a room with a window, a parapet and a patterned hanging, and the window side of the room is filled with gold. Which description of that panel is the most defensible?

options.text: The panel is late, since a gold ground in a picture of this date must be an archaism copied from an earlier work
options.misconception: converts the survival of a convention into a date, which conventions do not license

options.text: The panel is unfinished, since a window filled with gold is what remains when a painted view of a landscape was lost
options.misconception: reads a deliberate gold field as a lost landscape

options.text: The panel holds two systems at once, and the gold is the one that has not been given up while the room has been
The panel is a devotional image, since only a devotional image would place a reading woman in a room with a window
options.misconception: assumes a subject determines a function that a commission sets

questions.explanation: The interesting fact about a panel like this is that it is doing two things at once, and neither cancels the other. The room is a constructed interior: there is a window, a parapet, a hanging with a pattern, a seat seen in perspective, and light that falls consistently. The gold, on the other hand, is not a window onto anywhere. It is a surface, and it behaves like a surface: it is even, it takes no light of its own, and it gives the figure on the other side of the room a ground that does not recede. So the panel has a modern interest in the room and an older one in the gold, and the place where they meet is exactly where the meaning of the picture is generated. The gold side is not empty space; it is the space in which the reading happens, the world that the room opens into rather than the room that contains it. Three errors to reject. Gold in a window is a decision, not a loss, and there is nothing to restore. And a convention that survives into the 1480s is not evidence of date, because conventions are held onto for reasons that have nothing to do with chronology. The function of the panel is set by where it was made and for whom, not by the fact that a woman is reading. The test to apply: ask which parts of the panel measure space and which parts only state a surface, and accept that the answer may be both.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the panel measure a space and which only state a surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The monumental landscape of the Fan Kuan hanging scroll
questions.learningObjective: explain how scale and void distribute attention in a landscape scroll
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A hanging scroll in ink on silk, painted about 1000 and now in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, shows a single massive rock mass rising through most of the sheet, its surface built up with a dense grain of short strokes. Near the base, a mule train with a party of travellers is barely larger than the grains of the texture. A band of mist cuts across the middle, and above it the summit emerges. What is the arrangement of mist, rock and figures doing?

options.text: Composing a landscape, since a scroll of this kind was cut into sections to hang as separate pictures, so the sections are the composition
options.misconception: proposes a physical rearrangement that would not preserve the painting's sequence

options.text: Distributing attention, since the mist interrupts the mass and the tiny figures give the rock its size without competing for interest
Recording a journey, since a mule train crossing open country is the kind of detail a scroll uses to document a route
options.misconception: treats a staffage detail as a record of travel rather than as a measuring device

options.text: Creating depth, since the mist is a cloud lying in a valley and a cloud proves that the two masses are miles apart
options.misconception: supposes a single band of mist carries a specific measurable distance

questions.explanation: Three elements in this scroll do three different jobs, and keeping them apart is the whole analysis. The rock mass is nearly the entire field, and its surface is not smooth: it is built from a dense grain of short strokes that reads as the resistance of stone rather than as light falling on it. The mist is a band of emptiness cut across the middle, and its function is interruption. It breaks a single mass into two, so that the summit above it can be read as separate in space from the base below it, and it is the reason the eye can move up the sheet instead of stopping at the foot. The travellers are the smallest thing in the picture, and they are not there to be looked at. They are a measure, and a very efficient one: because they are the only part of the image at a known size, the rock can be read as enormous without any other device. Nothing is competing, because the figures are too small to hold the eye against the mass. The three wrong readings each turn a formal device into a claim it cannot support. A party of travellers is not a route; painters of this kind used such parties constantly, in mountains with no roads. A band of mist establishes that the two masses are separated, not how far apart they are. And a handscroll or hanging scroll is not a set of panels to be rearranged, because the sequence of its content is the sequence in which it is read, and reordering it destroys it.
questions.hint: Ask which element gives the rock its size and which element breaks the mass in two.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three distances of a dated Northern Song hanging scroll
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a signed and dated landscape from one dated only by inference
questions.stem: Written for this question, a hanging scroll in ink and colour on silk, dated 1072 and carrying a signature and a colophon, shows a valley seen from a high shoulder of rock, a middle-distance grove of leafless trees, and a far bank reduced by mist, with a stream running through all three. Trees on the near rock are drawn with fine downturned strokes, and the far bank is a few lines. Which feature of the sheet is the strongest evidence for the date?

options.text: The written colophon, since it is a statement made at or about the time of making, and the handling on top of it is a reading of that same tradition
The bare branches of the near trees, since winter tree drawing is recorded as characteristic of work after the middle of the eleventh century
options.misconception: turns a motif with a recorded currency into a date for a single sheet

options.text: The soft outline of the far bank, since a painter who dissolves distance into mist is following an older and therefore earlier manner
options.misconception: treats a stylistic inference as a date, and ranks the older manner as the earlier one

options.text: The use of colour, since a scroll with colour on it belongs to the later of the two traditions that divide this school's output
options.misconception: treats presence of colour as a chronological index, when both traditions use it

questions.explanation: A colophon is a different sort of evidence from a brushstroke, and the difference is worth being exact about. A written statement on the sheet, made by or for someone close to the making, is a claim about a moment in time. A stylistic feature is a claim about a body of work, and it will date a sheet to a range, not to a year. So where both are present, the colophon is doing the finer work, and the style is being used to check it: does this sheet's handling, the way the near rock is textured, the way the leafless trees are built from downturned strokes, the way the far bank is dissolved into a few lines, agree with what is known of that date and place? The three distances the sheet shows are a separate matter, and they are about construction rather than chronology. A high viewpoint looking down into a valley, a middle grove, and a far bank reduced by mist is a way of building a landscape in layers so that the eye can travel through it, and the same three-part scheme recurs in works of many dates. The three wrong answers are all cases of promoting a feature to a date. Colour was used in both of the schools that divide this output, so it discriminates between practices and not between centuries. Winter trees were a permitted subject, not a signature of a period. And an older manner is not automatically an earlier one, quite apart from the fact that a dissolve into mist is a technique rather than a period. The test: ask whether the evidence names a year or names a family of work.
questions.hint: Ask which piece of evidence on the sheet claims a year rather than a family of work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The empty foreground of a dated Yuan hanging scroll
questions.learningObjective: read an unpainted foreground as a positive spatial device
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A hanging scroll dated 1372, in ink on paper, shows a wide band of unpainted paper across the whole lower third, a cluster of trees at the far left, a small thatched building with a figure inside it at the right, and behind them a bank of low hills, with a few strokes of water and a distant ridge above. The paper is the lightest thing in the picture. What does the unpainted band do?

options.text: It is a loss, since the lower part of the sheet was cut away and the composition has lost its base
options.misconception: reads an intact, deliberate blank as physical damage

options.text: It is a sign of poverty, since only a small use of ink indicates a painter working without a full commission
options.misconception: infers economic circumstance from the quantity of ink on a sheet

options.text: It is a signature practice, since a painter of this date always left the lower third of a scroll unpainted
options.misconception: converts a choice into a fixed rule of a workshop

options.text: It is a foreground, since the blank paper reads as water or as a shore the eye crosses before reaching what is painted

questions.explanation: Unpainted paper in a Chinese scroll is not a hole, and the discipline of this painter is in leaving it. A blank lower band on a sheet of this kind reads immediately as water, or as a flat shore, or as the space the eye crosses before it reaches anything solid, and the reader supplies the connection between the bank in front and the ridge behind without being given a mark. That is the point of the device: the most economical way to say that a thing is far away is to make the viewer cross emptiness to reach it. Everything else in the sheet is arranged to make that emptiness do work. The trees are crowded to the left and the building is small and set to the right, so the eye is not held in the middle distance, and the few strokes of water and the low ridge above keep the far plane quiet. The building with a figure inside it is the only place where anything is actually occupied, and it is deliberately small, so the composition is about separateness rather than occupancy. The wrong answers are all ways of making a blank mean something it does not. The sheet is complete, and a composition is designed around its edges. Nor is a blank band a rule; painters of this generation fill the foreground as often as they leave it. And the amount of ink on a sheet is a decision about the picture, not a report on the painter's circumstances, which were not the subject of the commission.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is expected to supply in order to connect the near bank to the ridge behind.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a Song copy draws the figures of an early composition
questions.learningObjective: account for the drawing of a handscroll in terms of contour and wash
questions.stem: The description that follows was written for this question. A handscroll in ink and colour on silk in the National Museum of Asian Art, Washington, illustrates a poem about a river goddess. A long scroll opens at the right with a young man and an attendant on a bank, the river running away through a landscape of low hills. The figures are built from a thin, controlled outline, their garments and their long scarves described by a few long parallel strokes, and their faces left almost empty apart from the eyes and the hair; the colour is a pale wash inside the outlines rather than a layer over them; and the hills are stated in graded ink with almost no contour. What does the drawing do with the episode?

options.text: Recording the poem's metre, since the number of strokes in a garment can be counted against the lines of the text
options.misconception: supposes a stroke count that can be checked against a verse

options.text: Giving the figures the weight of a relief, since a wash inside a line can produce the solidity of a carved and painted panel
options.misconception: attributes a relief-like solidity to a convention of light colour on silk

options.text: Giving the figures the coherence of a design, since the scarves and the outlines run continuously across a long sheet and hold separate moments into one sequence
Fixing a date, since graded hills without contour belong to a period and a painter of that period drew them and no one else
options.misconception: turns a handling into a chronological index, which a copied design cannot supply

questions.explanation: The scroll has to do one difficult thing, which is to make a long sequence of short episodes hold together as a single designed object, and the drawing is how it manages that. A handscroll is read a short section at a time, at a distance of perhaps half a metre, with one hand unrolling, and each section has to be legible in a second and still recognisably continuous with the one before it. The thin controlled outline does that job: it is fast enough for a very long sheet and precise enough to be read at a glance, and because the same line describes the man, his attendant, the scarves and the water, the whole thing has one voice. The pale wash inside the lines rather than over them is the other half. It keeps the paper as the lightest thing in the picture, so the figures float against it rather than sitting in a coloured atmosphere, and it leaves the silk visible everywhere the painter did not touch, which is what lets the section boundaries fall between figures rather than through them. The hills, graded in ink with almost no contour, are handled the same way: they state distance without competing with the people. Two errors to reject, both of which the description itself rules out. A wash inside a line does not produce the solidity of a carved panel; the line remains a line and the silk remains visible. And no amount of counting of strokes will recover a poem's metre, since the two were not made in correspondence. The last error is the general one for a copy: whatever the handling is, it dates the sheet in hand, not a design that may be centuries older. The test to apply: unroll the scroll in your head and ask which element is doing the work of holding the sections together.
questions.hint: Ask which single element holds a very long sheet of separate moments into one sequence.

questions.topic: A narrative handscroll read at reading speed
questions.learningObjective: explain how a long scroll distributes events across a moving field
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A Japanese narrative handscroll from the second half of the twelfth century, in ink and colour on paper, tells the story of a monk whose bowl of rice is sent to a village each day by some power. In one section a granary lifts off the ground and drifts over a river, and the villagers run after it through open country; in another, travellers on a road stop and point upward, and the granary passes again behind them; in a third, a man on horseback and three others follow it across a hillside. The figures are drawn with quick, elastic lines and the ground is left open. What is the scroll's method of telling its story?

options.text: It alternates points of view, since each section is painted from the eye of one of the people in the story
options.misconception: assigns each section to a person, when the view stays outside the events

options.text: It places one event in each section, so the reader moves right to left and the same object reappears at different distances and from different angles
It builds one continuous landscape, so the river, the road and the hillside are parts of a single place and the events happen in order along it
options.misconception: supplies a single mapped place where the sections show separate settings

options.text: It uses scale to mark time, since the granary grows larger in each section and the growth stands for the passage of days
options.misconception: invents a chronological scale in a work where the scale tracks distance

questions.explanation: A long handscroll is a sequence of sections, and its method is to put one event in each, with a turn or a change of setting between them. The reader unrolls from right to left and the granary reappears each time, so the same object is the thread that holds the sections together while the setting around it changes completely. That is why the granary is drawn from different angles and at different scales in the different sections: those are the terms on which the scroll records where the thing is in relation to the people watching it, not how large it is in itself. The quick, elastic line is part of the same method. Figures are built from a few strokes that bend and repeat, and because the drawing is fast the eye reads it fast, which is what a scroll being unrolled at a walk needs. Open ground does the same work, since the emptiness between figures is what lets one group be read before the next arrives. The three errors each impose a structure the scroll does not use. There is no single continuous landscape, and the three settings are not parts of one map. Nor is scale a clock, which is a modern idea of measurement imposed on a device that is not making it. And the view does not move between people: the painter stays outside the events, which is precisely what allows one figure to recur and be seen from several sides, a thing a view from inside the action could not do.
questions.hint: Ask how many events a section holds, and what the changing size of the granary records.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The abbreviated brush in an attributed Zen ink painting
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what a traditional attribution asserts about a surviving scroll
questions.stem: Written for this question, a handscroll in ink on paper, in the Tokyo National Museum and traditionally attributed to a painter of the early thirteenth century, shows a man standing beside a stand of bamboo, one hand holding a brush and the other resting on his knee. The bamboo is drawn in a few rapid, broken strokes, the leaves in one or two marks each, and a great part of the paper is untouched. The scroll illustrates a well-known episode about a monk cutting bamboo as a way of training attention. Which reading of the abbreviation is best supported?

options.text: The abbreviation carries the subject, since the subject is an account of concentration and the fewest marks that hold it say that directly
The abbreviation is a convention for value, since fine painters were required to spend less ink on large works than on small ones
options.misconception: invents a rule about ink expenditure that no practice of this kind observes

options.text: The abbreviation is a copy, since only a copyist working from a pattern would reduce a tree to a few broken strokes
options.misconception: confuses a fast confident hand with a hesitant or dependent one

options.text: The abbreviation shows the work is unfinished, since a painter who meant to finish would have filled the empty paper with more bamboo
options.misconception: reads deliberate economy as incompleteness

questions.explanation: The subject of the episode is concentration: the monk takes up the brush to cut bamboo and finds that he cannot do it, and the moment of that failure, held in a single bent stroke, is the whole point of the picture. So an economy of marks is not a reduction of the subject, it is a claim about it. A hand that will not complete the gesture is a hand that has not mastered attention, and a painter who drew every leaf of the bamboo would be drawing a different episode, a diligent gardener rather than a distracted monk. The empty paper is part of this. A stand of bamboo occupies a few square inches of a long sheet, and the rest is left alone, so the eye is given nowhere else to go and nothing is allowed to compete with the figure. That is the same economy a good hand uses in any medium, and it is not a question of whether the work is finished. Two of the distractors confuse a fast hand with a weak one. A deliberate reduction is consistent from stroke to stroke across the whole sheet, which is the mark of a decision rather than of hesitation, and a copyist is copying a shape, not making a decision about what a subject needs. The fourth answer is simply a rule that does not exist, and the attribution named in the catalogue is a claim about the hand, not about the date, which the material and the tradition of mounting will have to settle on their own.
questions.hint: Ask what the episode is about, and what a painting of it would lose if every leaf were drawn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Stucco, calligraphy and light in the Hall of the Ambassadors
questions.learningObjective: account for how an interior room makes itself through surface and light
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A room built in the fourteenth century at the Alhambra near Granada has a low, tall, narrow hall with a roof of small stalactite-like cells in wood, walls whose lower half is a dado of glazed tile with geometric patterns, and above it a skin of carved stucco in which bands of script run across the surface among the ornament. Light enters through windows set high in the long walls, in a band of small openings. What is this room doing with surface?

options.text: Filling the wall, since every available surface was covered in this period and the density is a matter of custom
options.misconception: explains the density by custom and leaves the writing out of account

options.text: Reducing the light, since so many cut and carved surfaces would necessarily make the interior darker than an undecorated hall
options.misconception: supposes ornament works against the light when the high window band is arranged to exploit it

options.text: Imitating a woven tent, since a ceiling of small cells and a banded wall are the parts of a pavilion rather than of a building
options.misconception: proposes a source for the roof and the dado that the room itself does not require

options.text: Making the room's surfaces carry the programme, so the writing, the tile and the carved plaster together state what the room is for

questions.explanation: In a room like this the wall is not a background, and that is the fact to start from. The dado carries geometric tile, the zone above carries carved stucco in which bands of script are integrated with the ornament rather than applied to it, and the roof is a field of small cells that multiplies the effect of any light reaching it. So the whole interior is a single statement in three materials, and the statement includes what is written on the walls: the room says what it is in words as well as in shape. This is why the hall is a throne room and not merely a large chamber. The scale, the controlled admission of light through a high band of small openings, and the surfaces that catch and multiply that light all work on a visitor as he moves, and the writing makes sure the claim is legible to him. The three errors each reduce the room. Filling every surface is a custom, but a custom does not explain why the script is there, and the script is the part that carries meaning. The roof and the dado do not require an origin in a tent to be understood, and no one proposing such an origin has to reconcile the rest of the building. And ornament does not fight the light: cut and carved surfaces in a room lit through small high openings are a way of getting the light to register at all, since a flat wall would simply take the light and give nothing back.
questions.hint: Ask what the words on the wall are doing, and why the windows are set high and small.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A later Shahnama folio and the composition it repeats
questions.learningObjective: account for transmission in a repeated manuscript design
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A folio in a manuscript of the Shahnama held in an American university collection, dated 1562 and made in Shiraz, shows the legendary first king seated on a tiger skin with his court around him, all in leopard-skin garments, animals lying in the foreground, faces in the rocks of the mountain behind, and a sun with a face peeking from behind a crag. It is painted in opaque watercolour, ink and gold on paper. What does this sheet's relationship to a famous earlier version establish?

options.text: The date of the design, so a composition that appears in a document of 1562 must itself have been made in or before that year
options.misconception: concludes a design's date from the date of one surviving copy

options.text: The theft of a painting, so a painter who repeats a famous composition exactly has taken another's work without permission
options.misconception: reads the ordinary transmission of a workshop design as theft

options.text: The transmission of a design, so a book produced over a century later in a different city repeats the composition, and neither copy is the original
The workshop's originality, since a composition of this complexity could only have been invented once and then imitated
options.misconception: assumes complexity implies a single invention

questions.explanation: This sheet is dated 1562 and made in Shiraz, and there is a far earlier and more lavish version of the same subject made in the 1520s for a different patron in a different city. Putting the two together produces a fact about transmission rather than about either object. The composition travelled. A workshop design, built up over generations of book painting, was available to a scribe and painter in a southern city who had no access to the earlier manuscript and no intention of passing himself off as its painter. Both are legitimate: the earlier one is a first-rate execution of a shared design, the later one a competent and slightly different one. The details the description lists are the useful evidence here. The seated king on a tiger skin, the leopard garments, the animals, the faces in the rocks, the faced sun, and the small vignette of an animal attacking another are a set of motifs that recur across versions, so it is the design that is shared and not one picture. Three errors to reject. Repetition of a composition is the normal condition of manuscript production, not theft, and nothing here suggests deception. A date on one copy says nothing about when the design was invented, which is why the earlier date is evidence about the design's currency. And the complexity of a composition is not a claim to a single invention; such schemes are assembled from existing motifs over a long time. The test: ask which of the listed motifs also appear in other treatments, and you have identified the design.
questions.hint: Ask which of the described motifs recur in other treatments of the same subject.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The grounds of a thirteenth-century illuminated Hebrew page
questions.learningObjective: account for the material cost of an illuminated page
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A page from an illuminated Hebrew manuscript made in the Mediterranean about 1280 and now in a European library shows three compartments: a building with a pool and a lamp, a table laid with vessels, and an altar with a figure burning incense. The Hebrew text is written in a formal hand in lines of dark ink, and the compartments are filled with flat areas of colour with a limited range, and the whole page is squared off with ruled lines. What is the page's construction telling you about the book?

options.text: That the page was made to be read aloud rather than looked at, since ornament of this kind distracts a reader from the text
options.misconception: assumes ornament and reading are in opposition, which is the opposite of the case here

options.text: That the illumination is planned and budgeted, since ruled compartments and a limited palette are the marks of a page costed in advance
That the page is incomplete, since flat colour without modelling is the state a panel painting stops at when the shading is left out
options.misconception: carries a convention from another medium over to manuscript illumination

options.text: That the book is a copy, since ruled compartments are the standard way of recording an existing image for reproduction
options.misconception: reads a standard ruling practice as evidence of copying

questions.explanation: Look at what the description says about process and it becomes a document about how the book was made. The page is ruled into compartments before anything is painted, the text is written in a formal hand in even lines, and the colour is applied in flat areas from a limited range rather than modelled. Each of those is a choice that makes a page predictable, and predictability is what you buy when an illumination is planned rather than improvised. Ruling costs time in setting up and saves it in filling, and a restricted palette means the dyer and the painter could be supplied with a known set of colours. So the page is evidence of a book that was costed and divided in advance, which is exactly what a manuscript intended for a wealthy patron or for institutional use tends to be. Three errors need clearing. Flat colour is not an unfinished state; it is a normal and highly developed manner of manuscript illumination, and the convention of a shaded panel simply does not travel. Ruling is not a method of recording images for reproduction, it is a way of setting out a page. And ornament of this kind does not compete with the text. In a book like this the compartments and the writing are the same object, arranged so that the eye moves between the words and the pictures, and a reader who only read the text would miss the point of the page.
questions.hint: Ask which features of the page would be chosen before the pigments were prepared.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The throne and the gold ground of a late Duecento Madonna
questions.learningObjective: account for stacked scale in a devotional panel
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A panel painted in tempera and gold on wood, made about 1280 to 1290 and now in the Uffizi, shows the Virgin and Child enthroned and much larger than the church, the throne's builders, and two rows of prophets stacked in registers below and beside her, all on a gold ground, with the Virgin's face turned slightly away from the Child toward a ray of light from the upper corner. What is the stacked scale doing?

options.text: Measuring, since a small figure at the foot of a large one is a scale bar from which the heights can be calculated
options.misconception: treats a hierarchical arrangement as a measurable system

options.text: Perspecting, since the throne's side is drawn at an angle so that the eye can measure the depth of the seat
options.misconception: claims a constructed measure of depth in a field that declines to give one

options.text: Ranking, since the registers and the relative sizes set a hierarchy rather than a distance, and the throne is drawn to show that the hierarchy is a construction
Narrating, since each register carries a separate episode in the life of the Virgin and the order of the rows is the order of the story
options.misconception: assumes a sequence where the registers hold a single extended subject

questions.explanation: The figures on this panel do not share a space, and the panel is careful to say so. The Virgin and Child are set much larger than the church and its builders, who are themselves a good deal larger than the prophets in the registers below. That is not an error of proportion; it is a way of ranking, in which size states importance rather than distance from a viewpoint. And the throne is drawn to make the ranking legible as a made thing: its seat, its side and the hands of the small figures building it are all present, so the hierarchy is not being passed off as natural proportion but displayed as a construction the viewer is being shown. The gold ground then removes the last possibility of measuring anything, since it supplies no floor, no horizon and no recession. The turned face is part of the same apparatus, taking the Virgin out of a direct exchange with the Child and toward something beyond the panel. Three errors to reject. A figure at the foot of a large one is not a scale bar, and nothing in this arrangement can be calculated from. The registers do not narrate in sequence; they hold the prophets as an extended presence, which is not a story unfolding. And the throne's angle is not a measuring device: there is no consistent vanishing point here, because a consistent vanishing point is exactly what this kind of space refuses. The test: ask whether the figures would still be at those sizes if the Virgin were moved further away. They would, which is what makes the scale a rank.
questions.hint: Ask whether the small figures are far away or lower, and which of those the panel can show.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A technical report on the Sinai icon's join and media
questions.learningObjective: read a join and a medium list as evidence of design and of division of labour
questions.stem: A laboratory report on a panel icon in a monastery on Mount Sinai states that the flesh of the Virgin, the Child and both soldier saints is in pigment bound in wax and applied with a brush; that the garments, the background and the inscription are in a water-based medium; that the panel is of two boards joined vertically; and that the join runs straight down the centre of the Virgin's neck without entering the paint. What has the report established?

options.text: That the panel was assembled and drawn for this composition, and that more than one medium was in use, with the two chosen for what they do to flesh and to cloth
That the icon was repainted, since a water-based layer over wax is a sequence that only later restoration produces
options.misconception: treats the use of two media as evidence of a later hand

options.text: That the panel came from a joiner's shop rather than a painter's, since a cut board is the mark of a workshop that does not paint
options.misconception: supplies carpentry practice as a signature of a separate trade

options.text: That the icon was made in two campaigns, since the join's position behind the neck means the boards were cut at different times
options.misconception: reads a joint in a made panel as a chronological division of labour in time

questions.explanation: A technical report is worth most when each line answers a different question, and this one has three. The medium list says that two systems were in use and that they were chosen, not merely available: wax-bound paint worked with a brush can be modelled in the flesh, and a water-based medium is well suited to the flat, opaque cloths and to a legible inscription. The fact that the two were allocated to different parts of the picture is evidence of decisions, not of a shortage or a substitution. The join says something different and equally useful. A board joint running straight down the centre of the Virgin's neck, hidden under the paint, is not where a join would fall by accident: a maker who joined two boards without a drawing would not reliably place the seam behind the focal point of a face. So the boards were selected or turned to suit a composition, which is strong evidence that the picture was planned for this panel. Two of the distractors confuse manufacture with chronology. Nothing about using two media implies a later hand, since using two is a solution to a problem of surface. And a cut and joined board does not indicate a trade that does not paint, because panel preparation was part of the same commission. Nor does a joint date anything: a seam has no time in it. The general rule: a join tells you about design, a medium tells you about method, and neither is a date until it is compared with something else.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three findings is competent to establish, and keep the three apart.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Purple-dyed vellum in a manuscript catalogue entry
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a costly support establishes from what it does not
questions.stem: A catalogue entry for an illuminated manuscript reads: Genesis, in Latin; made in the early sixth century; ink and colours on purple-dyed vellum; the page 27 by 32.5 centimetres; ninety-six leaves. On the page opening the book, a short text in rustic capitals in gold sits above a painted zone of narrative scenes. What does the entry's statement about the support establish?

options.text: That the book is a copy, since only a copy would be made on a support too precious to waste on an original
options.misconception: assumes costliness argues against originality

options.text: That the pages were reused, since a purple ground is what remains when a paler sheet has been recoloured
options.misconception: reads a deliberate expensive dyeing as a later recolouring

options.text: That the book was made in a city where purple dye was traded, since the dye has to come from where it was grown
options.misconception: infers a place of production from the presence of a traded material

options.text: That the support was dyed before it was written on, which is a claim about expense and about the standing of the book rather than about its date or its place

questions.explanation: Purple is a claim about expense, and the direction of the claim matters. To dye vellum purple the skins have to be prepared, the dye applied, and the colour fixed, all before a single word is written, and a dye that produced this result was among the most costly materials in the trade. So the entry is telling you that the book was commissioned at a level where the support itself was a display, which is consistent with the gold capitals and the painted zone beside them: the whole object is arguing its own value. What the support does not do is date the book or place it. Dyeing is a technique, and techniques travel with manuscripts, patrons and materials merchants, so purple vellum is a fact about expense and not a fact about origin or moment. Two of the distractors get the direction of inference backwards. A material's presence tells you it was obtainable in quantity by whoever made the object, not that the object was made where it grows; and costliness is a reason to produce a book carefully, not a reason to copy one. The third is simply a confusion of process with damage: a sheet dyed purple before writing is what the entry describes, and there is no paler sheet underneath waiting to be recovered. The test: for every material named in a catalogue entry, ask what it cost, and then ask separately what it dates. Those are two different questions and the entry answers the first one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the dyeing happened before or after the writing, and what that ordering tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A dynastic label and an estimated date in one catalogue line
questions.learningObjective: read a period label and a date estimate as claims of different strength
questions.stem: A catalogue entry reads: Shiva as Lord of Dance; India, Tamil Nadu; Chola period; about the late eleventh century; copper alloy; height 68.3 centimetres; the ring of flame 56.5 centimetres across. Why does the entry give both a dynastic label and an estimated date rather than a single firm date?

options.text: Because the object was made for more than one patron, so a single date could not describe a commission paid in instalments
options.misconception: invents a payment history that the two lines do not describe

options.text: Because the alloy has not been analysed, so the dynasty is inferred from the metal and the century is a guess
options.misconception: assumes a link between alloy and dynasty that the entry never states

options.text: Because the dynasty is a well-founded container of dates while the object within it is an estimate, and the two are offered as claims of different strength
Because the dynasty name is the less reliable of the two and the object needed a firmer substitute for it
options.misconception: reverses the relative reliability, when a dynasty label is normally the broader and safer claim

questions.explanation: A catalogue entry that carries two dates is telling you it has two claims of different quality, and reading them as one is the mistake. A dynastic label is a broad container: a dynasty covers a span of a few centuries, and an object assigned to it shares a body of features, a workshop system, a foundry practice and a set of documented commissions, which is a great deal of evidence and reasonably firm. A century within that dynasty is a much narrower claim. Nothing on a cast bronze carries a year, and the argument for a late eleventh-century date rests on comparison with other objects of known or reasonably established date, on the alloy, on the casting, and on the iconographic and stylistic detail. All of that is real and it is also an estimate, so the entry writes it as one. Giving both is the honest arrangement, and it is also more useful than a single year would be, because a reader who needs to know how secure the date is can see that the secure part is the dynasty and the estimated part is the century. The distractors each invent a mechanism. The dynasty is the broader and generally safer claim, not the weaker one, and it is the century that needs the hedge. Nothing about instalments follows from a pair of dates. And nothing in the entry ties the alloy to the dynasty; the alloy is a material description, and a date is argued from a whole set of features together, not from one of them alone. The test: ask what evidence would move each claim, and you will see they are not the same evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what would be needed to overturn each of the two claims in the entry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The inlaid inscription on the base of the bronze David
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what an inscribed panel can and cannot establish about a cast
questions.stem: A record of a bronze figure in Florence, made about the 1440s, notes that it stands on a base whose front face carries an inlaid inscription in gold letters giving the name of the artist in a possessive form and the city he worked in. The inscription is complete and undamaged, and the surface of the base around it is continuous with the rest of the casting. Does this inscription settle when the bronze was cast?

options.text: Yes, because a gold inlay of this kind could not have been added later without visible disturbance to the bronze around it
options.misconception: assumes the technique itself rules out later insertion

options.text: No, and it is part of the argument, so it is weighed with the figure's dress, the hat, the boots and the costume against each other rather than taken as a verdict
No, because a gold inscription is a feature of many works of the period and so identifies nothing at all
options.misconception: generalises a common practice into a claim that it carries no information

options.text: Yes, because the name is in a possessive form, and an artist who wished to forge a later date would not choose to sign in that form
options.misconception: reads a grammatical choice as a security feature against forgery

questions.explanation: The honest answer is that the inscription is evidence, and evidence of a peculiar kind, so it belongs in the argument rather than at the end of it. Three features of the record limit what it can carry. It is a name and a city, not a date: it asserts who and where, and the question of when has to be argued from the figure and its setting rather than read off the plate. It is an inlay, and an inlay is a separate operation from a casting, so continuity of surface around it shows that the panel was set into a prepared recess, not that it was cast in the same moment as the figure. And the whole body of evidence on this work is genuinely divided: the antique precedent of a free-standing nude, the wide hat and the soft boots and hose that are nothing an antique would carry, the setting of a courtyard, and the possibility that a bronze was recast or a base recut. On those terms the inscription is a strong element and not a conclusion. Two of the distractors overrate it in opposite ways. A well-made inlay can certainly be inserted into a later base, and nothing in the record rules that out. And the form of a signature is a convention, not a security device; forgers do not avoid grammatical habits. The fourth answer is equally wrong: the fact that many works of the period carry such inscriptions does not make this one uninformative, since the question is what it says alongside other evidence, not whether the practice is common.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of claim the inscription is making, and whether a cast bronze could carry a plate added later.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The measured width of a hinged altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: infer a viewing condition from the recorded dimensions of an object
questions.stem: A survey of an altarpiece made in 1432 records: twelve painted panels set in a single hinged frame; 470 centimetres across and 350 centimetres high when the wings are open; the wings hinged at the outer edges with paint on both faces. A visitor can stand where the figures of the central panel are at eye level and can reach the outer panels with an outstretched arm. What follows from the measurements about how the object is meant to be read?

options.text: That the object is read by moving, since at that width the picture exceeds the field of view and the sections arrive in sequence as the visitor travels
That the object was designed to be seen in a photograph, since a single frame of that size is what a wide lens records without any distortion
options.misconception: assumes a twentieth-century camera to be the viewing condition a fifteenth-century object was built for

options.text: That the wings were an afterthought, since a frame this wide would have read as a single picture without any need to open anything
options.misconception: supposes a wide frame removes the need for shutters, when a field of that width is the problem rather than the solution

options.text: That the figures are unusually large, since a panel of that height cannot hold more than two figures of life size
options.misconception: puts an arbitrary limit on how many figures a panel of a given height can carry

questions.explanation: A width of 470 centimetres is a statement about a body. It is wider than a pair of outstretched arms, and a person standing in front of it cannot take the whole composition into one field of view, so the picture is delivered in parts. That changes the reading. Instead of one glance there is a traversal: the eye enters at one side, the sections arrive in an order that a person walking establishes, and the central panel is reached rather than seen. The height of 350 centimetres is a second condition and a more specific one, because it puts the middle of the composition at about the level of a standing adult. So the visitor is neither looking up at a frieze nor down at a plinth, and the figures in the central register are met at the height where another figure's head would be. The two measurements together define a reading condition, and that condition is the reason the frame is hinged at the outer edges: a work of this width that could not be opened would have to be read in fragments permanently. The three errors each misread what a measurement is. A wide lens is a later apparatus, and it flattens precisely the thing that matters here, which is the sequence. And nothing about a height of 350 centimetres limits the number of figures a panel may hold, since panels of that height routinely carry five or six standing figures. The general point is that dimensions are evidence about a viewing condition, and a viewing condition is evidence about what the work asked of a viewer.
questions.hint: Ask what a person can take in at one glance, and what that forces the object to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A comparison of four early manuscripts by material and placement
questions.learningObjective: read a table of attributes as a statement about shared priorities
questions.stem: A table of four books reads. A: a Gospel book of about 715 to 720; four evangelist portraits; no narrative pictures; no gold; one standing figure and a bird inside the initial of its first page, with a grid of animals around it. B: a Gospel book of about 800; no evangelist portraits; no narrative pictures; no gold; its first page carries monumental letters built from interlace, with cat and mouse forms in the field. C: a Gospel book of about 816 to 835; four evangelist portraits; no narrative pictures; no gold; each portrait is a single figure set in a landscape, drawn with a thin hooked line. D: a Psalter of about 830; no evangelist portraits; drawings beside nearly every verse; no gold; single figures in outlined settings, drawn in pen. Which reading of the table is best supported?

options.text: That portrait subjects are the deciding feature, since the two books with portraits belong to one tradition and the two without to another
options.misconception: makes a genre requirement that follows from a book's contents look like a marker of a school

options.text: That the earliest book is the least accomplished, since an inhabited initial is a simpler solution than a single full-page figure
options.misconception: ranks complexity backwards, when fitting a figure inside a letter is the harder solution

options.text: That the books fall in a sequence, since the image moves steadily from the initial to the full page as the dates advance
options.misconception: invents a progression out of a table whose dates and placements do not run in step

options.text: That all four decline gold and place the image differently according to what the book is for, so the constant is the drawn line and the variable is the placement

questions.explanation: Read down the columns first and the table says something clearer than any single row. Gold is absent from all four books, across a spread of more than a century and across two kinds of book, a Gospel book and a Psalter. That is a shared priority: these workshops spent on the drawn line rather than on a metal ground, and a table is the right form in which to notice a refusal that no single object would reveal. The variable is placement. Book A puts the image inside the opening letter of a Gospel, so a reader meets it at the moment of starting a book; book B goes further and makes the letters themselves the image, with no human figure at all; book C gives a whole page to a single evangelist in a landscape; and book D, being a Psalter rather than a Gospel, distributes drawings through the text so that reading and looking are interleaved. So the table shows a common restraint and a deliberate adaptation to the function of each book, which is the more interesting of the two findings. The three wrong readings fail in characteristic ways. A progression from initial to full page is invented: the dates do not run in the order of the placements, and book D is later than B while placing its images in the opposite way. Portrait subjects do not divide these books into two traditions, since whether a Gospel book has evangelist portraits follows from what the book is for. And complexity is not rank. An inhabited initial is a harder solution than a full page, because the figure has to stay legible inside the strokes of a letter.
questions.hint: Read the columns before the rows, and ask which value is constant and which varies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The Descent from the Cross and the strips it is cut into
questions.learningObjective: distinguish evidence about an object's construction from evidence about its style
questions.stem: The panel that shows Christ's body being lowered from the cross inside a shallow, gold-backed compartment, painted about 1435 and now in the Prado, has been separated into five vertical strips and is now presented as a continuous surface again. First say what the strips tell you about the object, and then say what they do not tell you about the painting.

options.text: They record a period of neglect, since a work strong enough to survive being cut up was necessarily left in a poor state for a long time
options.misconception: infers a history of neglect from the fact that a cutting happened at all

options.text: They record a second campaign, since a panel that had to be cut was one that had already been painted and then enlarged
options.misconception: invents a campaign from a division that requires none

options.text: They record that a wide single panel was later divided and rejoined, and they say nothing at all about the handling or the date of the paint
They record that the panel was always five separate boards, and they show that the painting was designed to be read as five pictures
options.misconception: reads a later division as an original modular design

questions.explanation: The first half is what the strips establish. Five vertical strips, rejoined, tell you that this was conceived and painted as a single wide panel, that at some later point it was divided, and that it is now again presented as one surface. A continuous painted scene crossing all five strips, with the figures and the gold ground running uninterrupted across the seams, is positive evidence for the single-panel origin, because a work made as five boards would have had to design five pictures. The second half is the discipline. Cutting a panel is a physical event in the object's history, and it tells you about storage, transport, framing and dealing. It tells you nothing whatever about the hand that painted, the quality of the paint, the intelligence of the composition, or when the painting was made. Those are argued from the paint film, the drawing, the comparison with other work, and the documents, and a cut is not among them. This is the general form the question is testing: construction evidence and stylistic evidence answer different questions, and an argument that lets one stand in for the other will always produce a false date or a false attribution. The three distractors each add something the strips do not say, in three different ways. A division is not an original design. A cutting is not a history of neglect. And a division is not evidence of enlargement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the strips were part of the plan, and then ask what the paint layer would have to show for a date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The hat and the boots on the bronze David
questions.learningObjective: weigh accessory evidence above learned antique reference
questions.stem: A bronze made in Florence about the 1440s shows a young nude standing on a base, with a wide-brimmed hat on the head, and soft boots and hose on the legs; in the right hand a long sword, in the left a stone. The head is turned sharply to the left with the brows drawn and the lips shut, and the head is the most finished passage of the whole figure, while the hair, the sling and the legs are not. First say what the turn of the head and the drawn brows do, and then say why the hat and the boots are a sharper piece of evidence about where and for whom the work was made than the nudity is.

options.text: They make the figure look heavy, and the accessories are decoration, since clothing on a nude has no bearing on where the work was made
options.misconception: mislabels a concentrated turn of the head and dismisses costume as mere decoration

options.text: They free the figure for the viewer, and the accessories show the bronze was unfinished, since a nude ought not to carry any clothing at all
options.misconception: treats the presence of costume as evidence of an incomplete state

options.text: They put the attention somewhere other than where the body is going, and the accessories place the figure in a contemporary courtly setting that the antique precedent deliberately does not
They hold the figure still for the viewer, and the hat and boots are a copy from an antique statue, since such dress is common in earlier sculpture
options.misconception: invents a classical source for accessories that belong to the present

questions.explanation: The two halves answer two different questions. On the first: the head is turned away from the direction in which the body advances, the brows are drawn, the lips are shut, and the head is the passage the sculptor finished first. So the body and the attention are aimed at different things, and the figure is not walking anywhere; it is waiting, and the waiting is the whole of its attention. The face is the part that is resolved and the hair and the legs are not, and that ordering is the sculptor's judgement about where the meaning sits, not an accident of the order of working. On the second, the argument is about evidence of different kinds. A nude male figure with a sword is a learned reference to a repertory of antique subjects, and repertories are shared, portable and widely known, so the nudity tells you the painter was thinking about antiquity, which is a statement about ambition. A wide-brimmed straw hat and soft boots with hose are not in that repertory. They are the dress of the present and of a courtly outdoor setting, and they are the sort of detail a patron would recognise at once and a viewer two centuries later has to be told about. So the two point in different directions at once, and that combination is what makes the work hard to place: a figure quoting antiquity and dressed for its own century. Three errors to reject. A turn of the head with a drawn brow reads as concentration, not as weight or paralysis. Costume on a nude is among the most telling things a bronze can carry, not decoration and not incompleteness, and no antique statue wears a straw hat.
questions.hint: Ask which features belong to a shared repertory and which belong to a date and a place.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The cloister and the enclosed garden in a convent fresco
questions.learningObjective: infer a viewing condition from the setting of a fresco
questions.stem: A fresco painted about 1440 to 1445 at the head of a stair in a Florentine convent shows an angel and the Virgin in a plain arcade opening onto a small walled garden, with two other figures driven out of the garden at the back. The faces are young and ordinary, the Virgin's hands thin, and there is no altar and no throne. First say what the architecture and the garden do to the reading, and then say why the plainness of the faces suits where the fresco is.

options.text: They fix the event in a specific and limited place and attach a sign to the garden, and the plain faces suit a corridor that monks walked past daily
They add a narrative of expulsion, and the plain faces indicate a workshop that had no access to models and so had to invent features
options.misconception: supplies a technical deficiency where the plainness is a decision

options.text: They establish the date, since an arcade of that form is only recorded in buildings of the 1440s in that city
options.misconception: turns an architectural form into a date for the painting

options.text: They show the fresco is a sketch, since a work with no throne and no altar was a design that was never carried out in colour
options.misconception: reads the absence of furniture as an unfinished state

questions.explanation: Start with what the architecture is doing, and it is doing more than describing a room. The arcade is not a stage set for the event; it is the actual architecture of the building, the plain vaulted passage of a monastic house, and putting the figures inside it says that this happened here, in a working corridor, rather than in an idealised temple. The walled garden then attaches a sign: an enclosed garden is an established attribute of the Virgin in this tradition, and the two small figures driven out of it at the back carry the reference through to what the enclosure excludes. So the setting is simultaneously a real place and a coded one, and neither reading cancels the other. The second half follows from where the fresco is. A corridor is passed in motion, at walking pace, in a building where the people who see it every day are the people it was made for. A Virgin with a thin hand and an unremarkable face meets that traffic better than an enthroned and idealised figure would, because there is nothing in it to object to and nothing that belongs to another building. Two of the distractors make a deficiency out of a decision. The absence of a throne is not a sketch; the absence of the accessories that belong on an altar is what makes the scene fit a stair. Nor does an arcade date a painting, though a form of architecture can help place one. The faces are not invented from a lack of models: a painter working in a city full of faces has no difficulty finding them, and choosing not to idealise is a choice.
questions.hint: Ask whether the architecture in the fresco belongs to the building the fresco is in, and who walked past it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a fresco wall is a record of decisions taken under time pressure
questions.learningObjective: explain the working conditions imposed by a wall painted a section at a time
questions.stem: A wall in a chapel in Florence was painted in about 1425 to 1427, and a survey of the surviving surface records that it was completed in a long series of separate areas, each of which was finished within a single working day, and that a later campaign of corrections exists in a second layer. First say what working a day at a time does to the decisions a painter can make, and then say why that makes the finished wall a record of a sequence rather than of a plan.

options.text: It has no effect at all, since a wall can be re-plastered and repainted at any time and so imposes no real constraint on the painter
options.misconception: treats a finished wall as a reversible surface it is not

options.text: It dates the wall exactly, since the number of surviving day-areas is a count of days and therefore a count of years
options.misconception: offers a day count as a unit of elapsed time

options.text: It forces the eye to commit before the whole is visible, and the corrections become part of the surface, so the wall records a sequence of decisions and not a single resolved design
It guarantees a consistent result, since a painter who must finish each day cannot change his mind and so the plan is preserved intact
options.misconception: supposes a deadline removes the possibility of a change of mind

questions.explanation: The two halves are about a constraint and about a consequence, and the mechanism has to be stated precisely. Paint applied to wet plaster becomes part of the wall as it dries, so a working day is a unit of irreversible commitment: whatever is laid on in the morning is part of the wall by the evening. That has two practical effects and one theoretical one. Practically, the painter has to know the whole design at the start, because he cannot erase a figure he has finished in order to fit it into a composition he has not yet reached; the drawing for the wall is therefore settled in advance and transferred across it, which is why a wall of this kind carries a full preparatory scheme and why the joins between the day-areas can often be found as slight tonal changes. Practically again, and this is the harder case, a figure that has to join a wall already painted has to be adjusted on the spot, and a record of corrections is not a sign of incompetence but of a decision made under a deadline. Theoretically, the day-areas are also a record of who was in the workshop and when, because the sequence of areas follows the sequence of the design and the seasons of the year limit how much of the wall can be done before the plaster is no longer workable. So the finished wall is a palimpsest of decisions in an order, and a survey that can find that order can find the chronology of the work. Two errors to reject. A deadline does not prevent a change of mind, it prices one, and a correction is the cheapest possible form of it. And a wall cannot be re-plastered at will; that is a different technique requiring the removal of what is there. The last is a category error: a day is a unit of commitment, not a unit of elapsed time.
questions.hint: Ask what a painter cannot undo once the plaster has dried, and what that does to his freedom to revise.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which an open altarpiece is read
questions.learningObjective: sequence the states through which a hinged altarpiece presents itself
questions.stem: An altarpiece made in 1432 for a church in Ghent has twelve painted panels on one hinged frame. Put these four things in the order in which a visitor standing before it would encounter them.

options.text: The upper register of the inner face, where a central group of three enthroned figures sits above a continuous horizon with prophets and sibyls to either side
The inner faces of the outer wings, painted in grey with two standing figures carved in imitation of sculpture
The closed wings, on whose outer faces two donors stand with their patron saints in a shallow loggia
The lower centre of the inner face, where a wide Adoration of the Lamb is set below the horizon line

questions.explanation: The order is a sequence of states and of a movement within each state, and it starts before anything is opened. A visitor arrives at a shut object, so the first thing encountered is the outer face: two donors with their patron saints in a shallow loggia, sized and framed to fit the wall. Then the wings swing, and the first thing on the far side of the swing is not the large picture but the inner faces of the outer wings, grey and painted to look like sculpture, which mark the change of register at the threshold and tell the visitor that a different kind of image follows. Once those are past, the eye goes to the top, because the upper register of the open inner face is the highest and carries a central group of three enthroned figures above a continuous horizon with prophets and sibyls running out to either side; the horizon ties the whole register together and stops the central group from floating. And the reading then comes down to the lower centre, which is the point the whole structure is arranged around. That is the order the eye takes, and the order the hierarchy takes: the shut state, the threshold, the register that establishes the realm above, and the panel that everything else addresses. The reason it matters is that a work of this kind is not an image but a sequence, and a description that lists the panels without their order loses the argument the object makes.
questions.hint: Ask what a visitor meets before anything is opened, and then which panel everything else is arranged around.
