questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the campaign narrated in the Bayeux Embroidery
questions.learningObjective: sequence a continuous narrative from its opening omen to its climax
questions.stem: A band of embroidery about fifty centimetres high, worked in wool on linen about the 1070s, narrates a campaign of about seven months in one unbroken run. Put these five events in the order in which the band shows them.

options.text: A meal is set and afterwards a gathering stands with cups and a figure speaks to another, and a palace is then attacked and its occupants killed
A portent appears in the sky and is pointed out, and a fleet is then equipped and a great number of ships are launched and cross a sea
A crowned figure falls with an arrow in the eye and a figure beside him cuts his throat, and the field is then strewn with bodies
Soldiers climb the bank of a river and a fight follows, and after the fighting a messenger rides with news to the opposite shore

questions.explanation: The order is the argument of the band, and it can be reconstructed because the sequence is causal and the captions confirm it. It opens with a portent: figures in a ship look up and point at something in the sky, which the written statements identify as a star or a comet, and that omen establishes at once that what follows is divinely sanctioned. Then the equipment and the launching of the fleet, and the crossing itself, with the ships drawn in two groups and the sea rendered as a set of stitched lines the ships seem to float on. Then the meal: a table is laid, food is carried in, cups are raised, and a figure speaks to another, which is the last scene of peace and the point at which everything changes. Then the fighting, which begins with soldiers crossing a river and then holding the opposite bank, and a messenger carries the news back across the water. And the band ends at the climax with a crowned figure struck in the face and a companion cutting his throat, the deaths the whole campaign was for. The order matters because the embroidery is not a record of days; it is a narrative with a shape, a bet, a passage and an outcome, and reading any scene out of sequence turns a story into a list. The captions exist precisely to hold the sequence steady, which is why the words and the pictures are one work.
questions.hint: Ask what has to come first for the story to be a bet, and what the meal marks.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the episodes in a narrative handscroll
questions.learningObjective: sequence the scenes of a Chinese narrative handscroll
questions.stem: A handscroll in ink and colour on silk, traditionally attributed to a fourth-century painter and itself dated by its materials to the twelfth or thirteenth century, illustrates a poem in which a young man travels to the river, meets a goddess there, is carried with her, and is then set down again. Put these four episodes in the order in which the scroll shows them.

options.text: He is carried up with her onto a cloud, and they rise above the river and the trees below
The goddess appears beside the water and the two face one another, and he follows where she leads
The pair are parted and he is set down again, and the section closes with him alone by the water
The journey to the river, with attendants and beasts on the road and the water reached at the end of the section

questions.explanation: The scroll follows the order of the poem it illustrates, and that order is a sequence of approach, encounter, ascent and loss. First the approach: a party travels to the river, and the section is filled with the road, the attendants, the beasts and the gradual appearance of the water, which is where the eye is meant to arrive. Then the encounter, which is the pivot of the whole scroll: the goddess appears beside the water, the two face one another, and he follows where she leads. Then the ascent, the one episode in which the scroll abandons its usual ground: the pair rise onto a cloud and are carried above the river and the trees, and the shift in the way the section is drawn, with more air in it and less ground under the figures, is the picture's way of marking the change of state. And then the parting, the last thing a scroll like this shows, with the two figures no longer together and him left alone by the water at the close. The order is worth reconstructing because a handscroll is not a wall of separate pictures but a run of time read in one direction, and the sections are laid out so that the reader experiences the approach, the moment and the loss in that order. Read out of sequence, and the ascent and the parting produce an effect the poet never intended.
questions.hint: Ask which episode is the pivot, and what the last section of a scroll of this kind must show.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three tiers of a chapel fresco cycle
questions.learningObjective: sequence a narrative cycle by the registers it occupies
questions.stem: A chapel in Padua whose walls were painted about 1305 carries a narrative cycle in three horizontal tiers running the length of the side walls, and a separate scene on the wall by the entrance. Put these three parts of the cycle in the order in which the walls present them, from the highest tier down.

options.text: The tier of the infancy and life of Christ, which occupies the middle band between the two others
The tier of the parents of the Virgin, whose story opens the cycle in the upper band
The tier of the Passion, which runs along the lower band of the side walls

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by the registers themselves, and it is a narrative order and a spatial one at the same time. The upper band carries the story of the parents of the Virgin, which is the necessary beginning: their marriage, the announcement, the long childlessness, the journey to the town, and the events that make the birth possible. Without that the cycle has no starting point, and the painters put it at the top so that a reader's eye enters the story at its highest point and descends. The middle band then carries the infancy and life of Christ, from the birth through the childhood to the ministry, which is the part that needs the parents behind it. And the lower band carries the Passion, which is the part a chapel like this exists to show, put at eye level and below so that it is met on the way in and on the way out, and running the length of both side walls. The separate scene at the entrance wall, where the dead and the living are separated, closes the whole sequence and is placed where a visitor leaving the chapel passes it last. So the cycle is read in one direction, from the highest register down and around to the entrance, and the arrangement is itself an argument: the story of salvation descends, literally, onto the person standing in the room.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the story has to come first, and where a chapel like this places the part that matters most.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a gold apse denies the space the emperor occupies
questions.learningObjective: explain how a decorative surface makes a claim about presence
questions.stem: Explain why the apse mosaic at San Vitale, made about 547, gives no shadow, no drawn architecture and no perspective behind the two imperial figures, and say what that refusal does to the way the emperor is presented.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the mosaic actually offers the eye. There is a gold field laid in even courses behind and beneath the figures, no cast shadow anywhere on it, and no drawn building, and the apse is a curved half-dome with a band of windows above it. That is all. The gold is a surface and it is even: it supplies no cue for distance, no horizon and no floor, so the figures have nothing to recede from. The refusal is not a failure of technique; a mosaic of this period could render a receding pavement or a shadowed interior perfectly well, and the artists who made the apse were among the most capable in Europe. It is a decision about what kind of space the image occupies. Three things follow from it, and they are the substance of the answer. First, the space becomes a presentation rather than a place. Justinian is not standing in a church on a particular afternoon; he is holding a bowl of bread and offering it, and the gold takes the offering out of any hour and place, which is exactly what a figure in an apse above an altar needs to do, because an apse is a place of offering and the image states the offering rather than depicting it. Second, the gold flattens the distinction between the real and the represented. The real light of the apse falls on the mosaic from the windows above, and the mosaic answers it with a field that has no light of its own, so the light in the room and the light in the picture are two systems that meet at the surface. That is a theological claim about a boundary, made in material. Third, it removes the possibility of hierarchy by scale. In a space with a floor, a taller figure would be a nearer one, and a smaller one a further one, and rank would have to be argued by other means. On a gold field, size is free, and the emperor can be as large as he needs to be and Theodora's panel can be made to answer his. That is why the paired panels work: they are not two moments in one room, they are two statements of equal rank. The real architecture is not missing, it has simply been moved from the picture to the room, and the windows that light the half-dome do the work that a painted building would have done. A viewer standing in the church below is therefore looking at a picture that refuses to be a window and is asking to be read as a presence, and the material is the argument.

questions.explanation: An explanation of this kind has to work in two halves, because the question has two. The first half establishes what the mosaic actually offers the eye: a gold field laid in even courses, no cast shadow, no drawn building, and a real band of windows above the half-dome. From those facts a conclusion can be drawn about the kind of space, because a surface with no cues for distance cannot supply one. The second half then has to say what follows for the subject, and that is where a weak account stops too early. A refusal of depth is not a refusal of meaning. It removes the floor that would make one figure nearer than another, and with the floor gone the size of a figure is free, so an emperor can be made as large as an apse needs. Pair that with the plain fact that the apse stands above an altar, and the apparatus becomes intelligible as a claim about offering rather than about a room. The discipline to hold on to throughout is the separation of what is present from what is inferred: the even gold and the missing shadow are observations, the reading of them is an argument, and a good answer marks which is which rather than blurring the two.
questions.hint: Ask what a surface with no cues for distance can do for a scene that needs to happen somewhere.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an illusionistic chapel wall can include a skeleton in a tomb
questions.learningObjective: explain an illusionistic cutaway as a claim about where a viewer stands
questions.stem: Explain why a fresco painted about 1425 to 1427 on the end wall of a church in Florence shows a painted barrel-vaulted chapel cut open as if the wall had been removed, with a painted altar at the back, a standing figure of Christ on the cross, the Virgin and a bearded man beside it, the two commissioning donors kneeling outside the painted frame, and below the whole of it a human skeleton lying in a sarcophagus with its lid pushed back. Say what the cutaway is for and what the skeleton is doing in a picture of the Trinity.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the fact that a wall is solid, because that is what the painted hole is arguing with. The fresco shows a barrel-vaulted chapel as if the end wall of the church had been cut away: two real piers stand forward, the vault behind them is drawn in correct perspective with its coffers diminishing, and at the back, at the head of the room, is a small painted altar with a standing figure of Christ on the cross, the Virgin on one side and a bearded man on the other. The two donors are painted kneeling outside the painted frame, on the actual wall. So the picture is a join between two kinds of space, a real wall in front and an invented room behind, and the line where they meet is the line the donors occupy. That is where the skill is, and the reason the illusion works. A painted room seen through a painted opening requires the opening to be drawn as a hole and the wall around it to be left solid, and a painter who paints a window where a hole should be gets nothing. The perspective of the vault is not decoration; it is the instrument that measures the distance from the real floor to the painted altar, and it fixes the viewer's place as precisely as a sundial fixes noon. So the first thing the picture does is invite a member of the congregation to stand inside the Trinity, and the kneeling donors show the position that invitation produces. Now the skeleton, which is the part that undoes the invitation. Below the whole illusion, in a painted recess cut into the wall and equal in scale to the real piers, is a human skeleton lying on its back in a sarcophagus with the lid slid off. No attributes, no allegory, no putti: a body, on a slab, in the dark. And it is placed at the bottom, at the level of a real tomb, so it is the most materially convincing thing in the picture. That is the argument. Above, a heaven that opens and lets you in; below, the fate that is the same for everyone, including the two men painted kneeling who are named at the bottom of the wall. Put the two together and the picture is making a claim about time rather than about space, and the means it uses is the collapse of two incompatible scales: the donor is roughly life size and the skeleton is roughly life size, and they are in the same wall. The conclusion is worth stating because it is the kind of thing a cutaway is for. An illusionistic chapel is not a window opened onto a heaven. It is a hole cut through a real wall, and what fills the space behind the hole is a decision about what the viewer believes will be there. Two errors to close. The first is to treat the painted room as a stage set, which misses the point: a stage set is closed and the hole is open, and it is the openness that puts the donor inside. The second is to treat the skeleton as a symbol, as though a skull were a coded message; a skeleton in an open coffin is a statement made with a body, and it needs no translation. The test to apply: ask what the picture would be if the painted piers were removed, and the answer is that it would stop being about this wall and this viewer.

questions.explanation: The method for this question is to take the two structurally different things the picture does in turn, because they pull in opposite directions and the picture is the argument between them. The cutaway is first, and its purpose is to place a viewer. A wall is solid, so a painted room on the face of it can only be looked at. Cut a hole in that wall in paint, and a solid pier stands forward as a real object in front of a receding vault whose coffers diminish in correct perspective, with the actual wall left solid behind the donors. The line where the real wall and the painted room meet is the line the donors kneel on, so the picture joins two kinds of space and puts a member of the congregation inside the second of them. The skeleton is the part that undoes the invitation. A body in an open tomb is the plainest available image of what waits, it is drawn at life size, and it sits at the bottom of the illusion so that the most materially convincing thing in the picture is a corpse. Put the two together and the wall is arguing with itself, and the way it argues is a matter of scale rather than of subject: a donor and a skeleton are the same size and they share a wall. Two errors to close. The cutaway is not a stage set, because a stage set is closed and the hole is open, and the openness is what admits the donor. And the skeleton is not a code to be translated; a body in a coffin is a statement made with a body. The test to apply: ask what the picture would be if the painted piers were removed, and the answer is that it would stop being about this wall and this viewer.
questions.hint: Ask what the hole in the wall is for, and then ask what a body in a coffin at the bottom of it is doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the objects in a domestic annunciation are doing
questions.learningObjective: read a group of objects as a statement about a moment
questions.stem: Explain what the objects in a small triptych of about 1427 to 1432 do to the reading of the scene they share a room with, and say how the angel's position and the dropped vessel tie them to the same moment.

answer.exemplar: The panel shows a workshop room. There is a bench, a table, a fire, a towel on a rod, a candle burnt down, a hanging cloth, a bench, a mouse, and on the sill by the window a small wooden trap with a baited cup and a dead bird beside it; lilies stand in a jug on the table. The angel is coming through an opening in the wall with one knee already across the threshold, and the young woman in the red dress has turned and dropped the jug she was holding. Take the objects first and then the figures, and the design becomes clear. The objects are the reason the panel can be about a moment rather than about a place. Most of them are ordinary, and their ordinariness is load-bearing: a domestic interior is a room where somebody is at work, and the fact that a person is at work in it is what makes the interruption mean something. Two items carry more weight than the rest and they are not the same kind of thing. The lilies are a sign, and a conventional one, and they say who the young woman is without a label. The trap is a different order of object, and it is the most argued-over item on the panel: a small wooden trap with a baited cup and a dead bird, set on a windowsill, has been read as a figure for entrapment and for the danger that waits. Whatever a reader makes of it, the point stands that the painter put a trap in a room where nothing is being trapped, and the placement is doing the work. Now the figures, and here the panel is precise. The angel is not arriving. A knee is through the opening, a wing is inside, and the woman's hand has opened and the jug has gone down and a stream of water is on the floor. So the message has already landed, and the room is caught in the instant after, which is why the towel is still on its rod and the candle has burned low and the work is interrupted rather than finished. That is the formal mechanism that makes the objects legible: they are the residue of a habit that has just been broken. Two errors to close. The objects are not inventory, because a trap on a sill beside a dead bird is a sign and not a possession. And the amount of domestic detail does not make the room the subject, because the subject is what interrupted it, and the panel is about an arrival in a household that was in the middle of a morning.

questions.explanation: The question asks two things, and the second is the harder one, so an answer should not treat them as the same task. The first is a set of observations that can be checked: what the objects are, where they sit, and what the figures are doing with their hands. The second is a claim about a moment in time, and it has to be built rather than listed. The method is to look for the single feature that fixes the instant, and here it is the jug on the floor with the hand that dropped it, because an open hand and a fallen vessel cannot be read as anything but the instant after a shock. Everything else in the room can then be read as the residue of a habit just broken, which is a general principle about domestic narrative: an interruption is legible only through the state of the room it interrupts. A strong answer will also handle the two most-tempting misreadings, that the objects are a list of possessions and that the amount of domestic detail makes the room the subject, and it will say why each is wrong. And it will be careful with the trap on the sill, which is the most discussed object on the panel and the one most often over-claimed: a good answer notes that the reading is debated and then shows that the placement is doing the work whether or not the interpretation is accepted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the angel is arriving or has arrived, and what the untouched state of the room tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a Song handscroll is not the painting its attribution names
questions.learningObjective: separate a claim about a design from a claim about a surviving object
questions.stem: Explain why a handscroll in silk dated by its materials to the twelfth or thirteenth century cannot be the fourth-century painting its traditional attribution names, and say what the surviving scroll does establish.

answer.exemplar: Begin by separating the two claims that a name on a scroll usually fuses. The attribution is a claim about a design: it identifies the composition this sheet follows, and it carries with it a history of collecting, mounting and inscription that explains why the sheet is valued. The dating is a claim about an object: the silk has a range, the pigments have ranges, the technique has a range, and a signature by the painter would narrow all of them, and there is none here. Those two claims are compatible once you notice what a copy is. A handscroll that transmits a composition attributed to a fourth-century painter, made seven or eight centuries later by an anonymous workshop, is doing exactly what such workshops did for centuries: preserving a design that the attributed painter could no longer be shown to have executed, and preserving it in a form that readers wanted. So the scroll is not a damaged original and not a forgery. A forgery is a deception, a work made to be taken for something it is not, and nothing here is trying to be that. The strong formulation to reject is that a painting cannot be younger than the artist it is attributed to. That is true of a panel and false of a copy, and the whole distinction is what the case turns on. What the scroll does establish is substantial. It establishes a design in circulation, in a particular state of completeness, with a particular set of episodes, and it establishes that the design was still being copied and collected in the twelfth or thirteenth century, which is itself historical evidence about the prestige of the attribution. It also establishes what the composition is: a narrative handscroll in which a poem is illustrated as a sequence across a continuous landscape, with slender controlled outlines and comparatively light colour washes. The distinction to state at the end is the general one. A name on a label is a report about a history of belief; a support and a pigment analysis is a report about a thing. Ask of each which of the two it is, and the confusion disappears. Where they agree, you have a secure object and a secure design. Where they differ, as here, you have a copy, and the copy is the more interesting evidence, because it dates the design's survival rather than its making.

questions.explanation: The reasoning here is about the relationship between two kinds of claim, and the method to state is the separation itself. A name carried by a scroll is a report about a history of belief: it summarises what collectors, mounting inscriptions and later catalogues concluded, and it identifies a design. A date argued from silk, pigment and technique is a report about a thing in hand. An answer that does not separate them will be pushed into the absurdity that a painting is younger than the artist it names, and the way out is the category of the copy, which the answer should then define by contrast with the forgery. From that follows what the object does establish, and that part should not be treated as a consolation: a copy in a museum of Asian art is evidence that the design was still being produced and collected in the twelfth or thirteenth century, which dates the survival of the attribution rather than the making of the composition. A strong answer will also note what would change the conclusion, namely a signature or a documented provenance pointing to a hand of the fourth century, so that the reader can see the claim is testable. The last move is the generalisation worth leaving behind, that a label and a laboratory report are not the same sort of document and should be weighed differently for the different questions each can answer.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece of evidence is a report about, and how a copy differs from a forgery.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The area of linen in a long embroidered band
questions.learningObjective: compute the area of a support from two recorded dimensions
questions.stem: A record of an embroidered narrative band, worked in wool on linen, gives the linen as 68.4 metres long and 0.5 metres high. What area of linen does that represent, in square metres? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its height, so the calculation is 68.4 multiplied by 0.5, which is 34.2 square metres. The second route gives the same figure independently by scaling both dimensions up by a hundred: 6840 centimetres by 50 centimetres, and 6840 multiplied by 50 is 342,000 square centimetres. A square metre is 10,000 square centimetres, so 342,000 divided by 10,000 is 34.2 square metres, and the two routes agree because the conversion factor cancels against the one it is applied to. A third check is the simplest of all: a height of 0.5 metre is exactly half a metre, so the area is half the length, and half of 68.4 is 34.2. The number matters because of what it implies about the object. Thirty-four square metres of linen is a very large support, and a band of that size cannot be looked at whole by anybody. It has to be read in sections, unrolled a little at a time, which is precisely why the embroidery separates its episodes with written captions: the words are there because the surface is too long for a viewer to hold the sequence in one look. So the arithmetic and the art history are one claim, and a slightly different figure would weaken it: a band of a few metres would not need the apparatus this one has. Note also what the calculation is not. It says nothing about how long the work took, because the rate of stitching is not given, and nothing about how many people worked on it, because the workforce is a separate fact about the commission.
questions.hint: Multiply the two dimensions, then confirm by converting to centimetres and square centimetres.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The halo of a bronze figure as a proportion of its height
questions.learningObjective: compute the proportion of two recorded dimensions of a sculpture
questions.stem: A catalogue entry for a copper-alloy sculpture records a total height of 68.3 centimetres and a ring of flame with a diameter of 56.5 centimetres. What percentage of the total height is the diameter of the ring, to one decimal place? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: The proportion is the ring's diameter divided by the whole height, multiplied by one hundred, so the calculation is 56.5 divided by 68.3 and then by 100. That quotient is 0.8272327964860908, and one hundred times it is 82.72327964860908, which to one decimal place is 82.7. The same result comes from the reduced form of the fraction: both numbers are given to one decimal place, so multiplying numerator and denominator by ten gives 565 over 683, and 565 divided by 683 is 0.827232796, unchanged, because the scaling cancels. A check by the remaining height does the verification differently again: 68.3 minus 56.5 is 11.8 centimetres, and 11.8 over 68.3 is 0.1727672, whose complement to 1 is 0.8272328, exactly the ratio computed above, so the two parts of the height account for the whole. The figure is worth having because it says something about how the object works. A ring that is 82.7 per cent of the total height is not a background behind the figure; it is a container nearly large enough to hold the whole body, and the figure stands inside it rather than in front of it. That is why the halo is not decoration that could have been made smaller, and why the composition has to be read as a single unit: the ring and the figure are one object, dimensioned together. A proportion near one is the signature of a form in which the enclosure is part of the subject, and this is one of the clearest cases in which two catalogue numbers describe a single idea.
questions.hint: Divide the ring's diameter by the total height, multiply by 100, and round to one decimal place.
